chapters.title: The Ordinary Account
pages: At eight forty-five on Monday morning, Sophie Bennett was arguing about a delivery note with a man who had never seen the delivery note. He was a buyer at a small chain of garden centres, and he had been charged for six replacement tablets Northbridge Solutions had sent after a courier damaged the originals. Sophie opened the account, found the courier report, and explained that the invoice had been raised automatically before the credit was approved. She promised to send the corrected statement by lunchtime, then waited while he decided whether to believe her.
“You’re very calm about it,” he said at last.

“I’m trying to be useful,” Sophie replied. It was true, though not the whole truth. She was also watching the clock. Her meeting with James Whitmore, Northbridge’s commercial director, was in ten minutes, and she had spent the previous evening rehearsing what she would say about her next career step. She had prepared a short list of accounts she could take on. Meridian Retail Group was not on it. Meridian was not the sort of account anyone took on casually.

James’s office had glass walls and a view of the canal, which made private conversations feel faintly theatrical. He did not ask about her presentation. He passed her a folder and told her that Eleanor Shaw, the senior account director responsible for Meridian, was going to be away for several months. The renewal was due in fourteen weeks. Sophie would lead the account from that morning.
“Lead it or keep the wheels turning?” she asked.

“Lead it,” James said. “With support. Meridian is worth about £4.8 million in annual revenue to us. It is also one of our most visible contracts. If we retain it on poor terms, we can be worse off than if we lose it. I need someone organised, credible and prepared to listen.”
Sophie felt the pleasure first, then the fear. “Why me?”

“Because you know how to get answers from people who are cross. And because you’ve been asking for a bigger account.” James watched her take that in. “This is the bigger account. It is not a reward. It is a test.”

At her desk, Sophie read the contract summary twice. Northbridge supplied Meridian with store-support software, a service desk, field engineers and data integrations across 312 shops and three distribution centres. The current agreement had been signed for three years, with annual indexation and a service-credit schedule. Meridian’s renewal letter requested a substantial reduction in annual charges, tighter response and restoration targets, and greater flexibility to change the number of supported sites.

Sophie copied the requests into a spreadsheet and labelled the last column “Possible concessions”. She meant it as a working heading, but the phrase looked more decisive than she felt. She had not yet spoken to Meridian’s operations team, reviewed the incident history or asked finance what the contract actually earned. Still, a blank document had a way of inviting premature certainty.

Across the aisle, Oliver Grant, a junior analyst, was trying to get a report out of the service database. Rachel Singh from legal passed behind him with a marked-up contract under her arm. Martin Cole, Northbridge’s service-delivery manager, was on a call, explaining to someone that an engineer could not be in Leeds and Bristol at the same time. The company was not a single voice. Sophie knew that. She also knew that, in fourteen weeks, she would be expected to make it sound like one.

chapters.title: The First Position
pages: Meridian’s offices occupied two floors above a flagship shop near King’s Cross. Sophie arrived early enough to review her notes in the reception area, where a wall display showed live sales figures in carefully rounded millions. She had brought a service report, a price history and a draft agenda. James had advised her to ask questions before defending anything. She had written this at the top of the agenda in capitals.

Helen Carter, Meridian’s procurement director, greeted her with a brisk handshake. David Chen, operations director, joined them in a meeting room with a view of the railway lines. Helen placed a printed copy of Meridian’s renewal request on the table.

“We want a twenty per cent reduction in the annual charge,” she said. “We also need stronger service guarantees and the ability to flex the estate without a change-control exercise every time a shop opens or closes.”
Sophie nodded. “That’s a clear starting position.” She heard herself say it too quickly, as if clarity made the demand reasonable.

Helen explained that Meridian was under pressure to simplify supplier costs. Its retail estate had shifted since the pandemic: a handful of smaller sites were closing, while several larger formats were being tested. Procurement had been asked to find savings across every major technology contract. “We can’t pay for a fixed footprint when the business itself is changing,” she said.

Sophie opened her report. “The current service has delivered 99.84 per cent availability across the core platform, and the annual charge reflects the support coverage, integrations and on-site response model. A twenty per cent reduction would take us below the cost of delivering the service as specified.”
“Then the service as specified may not be what we need,” Helen said. “We’re not asking you to perform the same work for less. We’re asking for a different deal.”

It was a useful distinction. Sophie recognised it, but her attention had fixed on the percentage. She began listing Northbridge’s costs: the service desk, the regional engineer rota, the overnight monitoring, the third-party hosting fees. Each item was accurate. Together, they sounded like a defence of Northbridge rather than an enquiry into Meridian.

David leaned forward. “The headline availability figure is fine. What concerns me is recovery. In November, the Midlands distribution centre lost the dispatch interface for three hours. The system came back, but we had people reconciling orders manually for most of the afternoon.”
Sophie looked down at her report. It showed the incident as a priority-one event, restored within the contractual target. “The service report records a two-hour restoration.”
“The interface was restored,” David said. “The operation wasn’t. That’s the difference I’m trying to get at.”

Sophie asked whether the issue was the response time, the restoration time or the recovery process. David described the additional work his team had carried out and the lack of a clear status update during the incident. Helen watched Sophie closely. For the first time, Sophie wondered whether Meridian’s demand for stronger guarantees was less about punishing Northbridge than about being unable to explain operational risk to its own senior team.

“We can review the incident evidence,” she said. “And look at a more useful measure than platform availability alone.” Then, uncomfortable with the silence that followed, she added: “But we would need to price any material change.”
Helen closed the folder. “We haven’t agreed what material means, or what you would measure.”

Sophie said she would return with options. Helen said she expected a commercial response, not another account of Northbridge’s costs. David asked for the incident timeline and the recovery notes. The meeting ended after forty minutes without a price movement, an agreed service measure or a date for the next discussion.

On the train back, Sophie replayed the conversation and heard how often she had spoken. She had protected Northbridge’s position, but she had not established what Meridian needed to be able to do. A lower price might be a position; predictable operating cost, flexibility and confidence in recovery might be the interests beneath it. She opened her notebook and wrote: “Ask what they will trade. Do not assume the number is the problem.”
Then she added, after a pause: “Find out whether they would accept a smaller reduction for a different service design.”

chapters.title: The Cost of Keeping It
pages: James read Sophie’s meeting notes without interrupting. When she finished, he tapped the page where she had written “20%”.
“That’s their opening position,” he said. “It isn’t yet their reservation point, and it certainly isn’t our answer. What did they say they needed?”

Sophie recounted the changing store estate, the distribution-centre incident and the need to explain service risk internally. James asked what she had learned about Meridian’s budget cycle, who signed off operational changes, and whether the request applied to all suppliers or only Northbridge. Sophie knew the renewal deadline and the names in the room. She did not know the rest.
“You don’t have to solve the negotiation in one meeting,” James said. “But you do have to stop treating a demand as a diagnosis.”

He had brought in Priya Nair from finance and Martin Cole from service delivery. Oliver joined to take notes and pull the relevant data. Rachel, legal counsel, had sent her comments in advance and appeared by video for the first half-hour.

Priya displayed the current contract economics. Meridian’s annual revenue was £4.8 million, but revenue was not profit. Direct delivery costs, hosting, licences and allocated support came to about £3.75 million. The resulting contribution margin was just under twenty-two per cent, before central overhead. A twenty per cent price reduction with the existing service scope would remove nearly all that contribution.

“That doesn’t mean every discount is impossible,” Priya said. “It means a discount must be attached to a change in cost, risk or commitment. If we cut price and keep the same obligations, we are paying Meridian to remain our customer.”

Martin said the current agreement was expensive to serve in some areas and efficient in others. The engineer rota had to cover all regions even when site visits were rare. The service desk took a high volume of low-complexity requests, while a small number of integration failures created disproportionate disruption. He could redesign the model, but not safely by guessing.

Rachel’s voice came through the speaker. “Flexibility also has a cost. If Meridian can remove sites at short notice while Northbridge keeps the same dedicated capacity, the risk sits entirely with us. We can offer a quarterly adjustment mechanism, but it needs notice, bands and a minimum commitment.”

Sophie wrote down “reciprocal”. She had been thinking of concessions as things Northbridge might give to win the renewal. Rachel was describing them as exchanges. Better flexibility could be worth something to Meridian, but it would also require Meridian to commit to forecast accuracy, transition periods or minimum volumes.

James asked what alternatives each side had. Northbridge could reallocate some staff if Meridian left, but the transition would be disruptive and the lost revenue would matter. Meridian could extend parts of its existing arrangement, use another provider, or bring selected support functions in-house. None of those choices was effortless. Neither side was negotiating from a position of helplessness.
“Our alternative has a cost,” Priya said. “So does theirs. We should know both, without pretending either one is a threat.”

The team argued over service levels. Martin thought a guaranteed response time was feasible; a guaranteed restoration time for every incident was not, because Meridian’s own systems and third-party networks could be involved. David’s concern, Sophie said, was that the existing measures rewarded technical restoration while leaving operational recovery unmeasured.

They agreed to investigate a two-part service model: response and restoration targets for Northbridge-controlled issues, plus a defined incident-management process for wider failures. Service credits would apply only to failures attributable to Northbridge and would be capped. Martin wanted clear exclusions; Sophie insisted the reporting had to show the customer what happened, not merely why a credit did not apply.

When the meeting ended, Sophie had a list of tasks rather than an offer. She felt an unwelcome but useful shift in her thinking. Winning the renewal could not mean giving Helen every visible concession and hoping the numbers worked later. It would mean finding a structure both organisations could operate—and making sure each improvement had a counterpart.

chapters.title: What the Numbers Conceal
pages: For the next three days Sophie treated preparation as if it were a form of control. She asked Oliver for twenty-four months of incident records, then checked his classifications against Martin’s operational logs. She requested the invoices for third-party hosting and licences. She read the contract’s change-control clauses and marked Rachel’s comments in the margins. At home, she built a spreadsheet with three commercial scenarios and colour-coded the cells until the figures seemed almost reassuring.

Oliver found that the headline availability figure concealed a pattern. Most incidents were brief and resolved within target, but five had caused meaningful disruption to Meridian’s distribution or store operations. In three cases, the platform had been available while a connected process remained impaired. The contractual report did not capture the full recovery period.
“The data isn’t wrong,” Oliver said, “but it answers a narrower question than David was asking.”

Sophie thanked him and asked him to add a column for operational impact, with the source of each estimate clearly stated. She was learning that a useful report did not merely make Northbridge look good.
At their next internal review, Priya challenged Sophie’s first scenario. It offered a twelve per cent reduction in annual fees, paired with reduced on-site coverage and a two-year extension.
“What does Meridian give us in return?” Priya asked.
“A longer term.”

“A term is not automatically valuable if they can still remove sites whenever they want.” Priya pointed to the draft. “And we haven’t costed the transition between service tiers. You’re offering a discount before you’ve established the baseline.”

Sophie felt the old instinct to defend her work rise, then set it aside. She replaced the single percentage with a pricing framework: a fixed core charge, a variable site component, and a limited adjustment window each quarter. The fee would fall if the supported estate contracted, but only within agreed bands and with notice. Larger changes would trigger a review and a transition plan.

Martin was less comfortable with the service proposal. Sophie had written a target for restoration of priority-one incidents and an improved service-credit schedule. He pointed out that a numerical target could be misleading if an issue depended on Meridian’s network or a software supplier.
“Then define the clock,” she said. “And define what happens when the clock is paused. But don’t make the reporting so full of exceptions that David cannot use it.”

They settled on separate measures for acknowledgement, response and restoration, with a joint incident review for severe events. Northbridge would provide regular updates during a priority-one incident and a written cause-and-recovery report within five working days. The draft did not promise that every operational consequence could be eliminated; it promised clearer ownership and evidence.

Rachel reviewed the service-credit language and warned that credits were a remedy, not an insurance policy. Sophie agreed. She did not want a generous credit that concealed a weak service design, or a guarantee so narrow that Meridian would regard it as theatre.
James asked her to rehearse the commercial conversation. Sophie began with the cost of the current arrangement, then stopped herself.
“I’m explaining our position again,” she said.
“You are,” James replied. “Try asking what a workable change looks like to them.”

Sophie practised: “If we separate the fixed platform and integration costs from the variable site support, would that help you manage an changing estate? What commitment could Meridian make in exchange for greater flexibility?” She replaced “an changing” with “a changing”, and James let the correction pass without comment.

She also prepared questions about the twenty per cent: whether it was a target, a budget requirement or an instruction from the board; whether Meridian would consider a lower reduction in year one if the service measures improved; and what evidence David needed to trust those measures.

At the end of the session, James told her she had enough to take a proposal into the room, but not enough to present it as the answer. Sophie gathered the papers. Her carefully coloured spreadsheet no longer looked like control. It looked like a map of what she still needed to learn.

chapters.title: A Better Question
pages: Sophie returned to Meridian with no completed offer. She had brought a one-page outline, the verified incident analysis, and a table showing how different levels of site flexibility would affect price and delivery cost. She had also left several figures blank. James had advised her not to fill them merely because an empty cell made a meeting feel unfinished.
Helen glanced at the outline. “I thought you were coming back with a commercial response.”
“I am,” Sophie said. “But I don’t want to put a price against a service model you haven’t agreed is useful. I’d like to test the structure first, then send a priced proposal within two working days.”

Helen studied her, as if deciding whether this was discipline or delay. David opened the incident analysis. “This is the first report I’ve seen that separates technical restoration from operational recovery.”

They discussed the November outage in detail. Sophie did not argue that Northbridge had met its contractual target. She explained where the service desk had identified the failure, where updates had been delayed, and how the handover between the platform team and Meridian’s distribution staff had lacked a clear owner. David said the technical team had been responsive once engaged, but Meridian had not known who was coordinating the wider recovery.
“We can put a named incident lead in place for priority-one events,” Sophie said. “And set an update rhythm, even if the cause sits outside Northbridge’s control.”
“Would that be included?” Helen asked.
“For the contracted priority-one response, yes. A dedicated resource around the clock would be different, and I wouldn’t want to imply otherwise.”
That answer seemed to reassure David more than an unqualified promise would have done. He asked for the proposed reporting format and the definition of a priority-one event. Sophie wrote both down.

Helen returned to the price. The twenty per cent reduction, she said, was the ambition her leadership team had given procurement. It was not a simple instruction to accept any service cut. The group had to absorb a rise in logistics costs and needed predictable spend. “A reduction that disappears when the estate changes is not a saving I can defend,” she said.

Sophie asked whether predictable spend mattered more than the precise year-one reduction. Helen paused. “It matters alongside it. I still need a material reduction. I also need to show that any flexibility is not a blank cheque.”

The exchange made the interests clearer without making them easier. Meridian wanted lower cost and room to alter its estate; it would not accept new charges every time a shop closed. Northbridge needed a viable margin and enough notice to plan capacity. David wanted operational confidence that the existing service measures did not provide.

Sophie proposed separating the fee into a fixed platform and integration charge, and a variable site-support charge. Meridian could adjust the number of sites within agreed quarterly bands, with advance notice and a minimum annual commitment. If the estate changed beyond the bands, the parties would review the service model rather than trigger an automatic price cut.

Helen said the mechanism might work, but asked for the numbers. Sophie did not offer the twelve per cent she had written in her first draft. That figure had been built on assumptions about reduced coverage and an extension Meridian had not promised. Instead, she said Northbridge could model a material first-year reduction against the current fee if Meridian accepted the defined bands, a minimum commitment and a two-year renewal. The actual reduction would depend on the confirmed site baseline and the chosen coverage.
“So you’re not offering the twenty per cent,” Helen said.

“Not for the current scope, no. I am saying we can test a different scope and cost structure. If the reduction is the only acceptable outcome, we should say so now rather than trade figures without a basis.”

David asked whether the service-credit cap would rise. Sophie said Northbridge could review the cap in exchange for the revised incident process and a clear distinction between failures it controlled and those it did not. Helen wanted the credit schedule to carry real weight. They did not settle the detail, but they agreed that a credit would not replace the operational review.

When the meeting ended, Helen had not accepted a proposal and Sophie had not secured a renewal. They had, however, agreed that Sophie would send two priced options, with the assumptions and trade-offs stated plainly, by Friday. David would provide Meridian’s forecast of site changes; Helen would confirm the budget range she could take to her leadership team.

Back at Northbridge, Sophie sent James a short account of the meeting. She did not call it progress in the subject line. She wrote that the parties had identified a possible exchange: lower and more predictable pricing against minimum commitment and notice, with stronger incident ownership against a service model that could be costed. Then she opened the spreadsheet and began again, this time leaving room for Meridian to say no.

chapters.title: The Shape of the Evidence
pages: By half past eight, the meeting room at Northbridge Solutions had acquired the air of a small control centre. Priya had put the support-ticket data on one screen and the contract’s service schedule on another. Sophie stood between them with a notebook open, while James poured coffee nobody had asked for.
“We have three years of tickets,” Priya said. “Or rather, three years of records that people have agreed to call tickets.”
James glanced at her. “That sounds reassuring.”

“It isn’t meant to.” Priya enlarged a column of figures. “Meridian logged 1,842 incidents last year. Our system shows 1,316. The gap is mostly duplicate entries, requests sent to the wrong queue, and cases closed by Meridian before we could verify the fix.”
Sophie read the labels. Some discrepancies were plainly procedural; others were not. “Can we separate them without making the categories do more work than the evidence?”

“I’ve started. Of the 526 unmatched cases, 214 have a clear duplicate or routing explanation. For 137, there’s no reliable record beyond an email thread. The rest are mixed.” Priya paused. “I can defend the method. I can’t claim the result is perfect.”
“Good,” Sophie said. “We shouldn’t present uncertainty as a saving.”
James leaned over the table. “But the overall trend is favourable. Northbridge response times improved by eleven per cent.”
“Against our own clock,” Priya said. “Meridian’s clock starts when the store reports a problem. Ours starts when the case reaches the correct support queue. The difference matters.”

Sophie looked again at the two screens. In the earlier sessions, both sides had argued from headline figures: Meridian’s demand for a lower annual fee, Northbridge’s insistence that the existing price was already tight. Here, under the labels, were several separate disputes—what counted as an incident, who owned the first response, when the clock began, and what a timely resolution meant. They could not be settled by choosing the more persuasive total.

“Let’s make a reconciliation table,” she said. “Show the agreed records, the disputed records, and the reason for each dispute. Then we can talk about what the service actually needs, rather than whose spreadsheet wins.”
James gave a small nod. “And the cost position?”

Priya switched windows. “The account revenue is £4.8 million a year. Direct delivery costs are about £3.94 million. That leaves £860,000 before central overheads, which is an eighteen per cent contribution margin. Not eighteen per cent profit.”
“The distinction will be lost if we put it in a slide,” James said.
“Then we should put it in the slide,” Sophie replied.

The contract renewal was due in four months. Meridian had signalled that its board expected a reduction in operating costs, and Helen had repeated that expectation in the previous session without specifying a target. Northbridge had already offered to hold its annual fee at £4.8 million for a further year, provided the scope remained stable. Meridian wanted a lower price and clearer accountability; Northbridge wanted predictable demand and fewer avoidable incidents. Neither position was the same as the interest beneath it.

“There’s one more finding,” Priya said. “Seventy-three per cent of the tickets classed as integration failures arrived during the overnight stock update. But we can’t establish whether the fault sits in our connector, Meridian’s data feed, or the hand-off between them.”
“Can you establish the cost?” Sophie asked.
“Not cleanly. We estimate £96,000 a year in extra support and manual checking. There’s a range of about forty thousand either way.”
James whistled softly. “That would make a useful efficiency number.”
“It would make a useful hypothesis,” Priya said. “If we call it a saving before we know the cause, we’ll be arguing about a number we invented.”

Sophie wrote: validate before pricing. “We can propose a joint diagnostic, with access to both systems and a named owner on each side. If it finds a Northbridge fault, we fix it within the service plan. If the cause is outside our scope, we agree a change before anyone starts charging.”
“And if it finds both?” James asked.
“Then we allocate responsibility by evidence, not by which team has the louder voice.”

She could see that James was considering whether this sounded too cautious. He had spent the first two meetings defending Northbridge’s competence. Sophie understood the impulse. Yet confidence that ignored an uncertain hand-off would become brittle as soon as Meridian produced a different record.
“What do we show Helen?” James asked.
“The trend, with its definition. The gap, with its explanation. And the uncertainty, without pretending it is a concession.”
Priya smiled. “That may be the least glamorous slide deck I’ve ever made.”
“It may also be the first one they trust.”

Before the meeting, Sophie sent Helen a short note attaching the proposed reconciliation categories. She did not claim that the data proved Northbridge had met every obligation. She said it supported improvement in response times, while leaving the timing and ownership of a significant group of incidents unresolved. She asked whether Meridian would nominate someone to take part in a joint review.
Helen replied ten minutes later: “Rachel can join. Please keep this separate from the commercial offer.”
Sophie read the sentence twice. It was not a refusal. It was a boundary, carefully drawn. She forwarded it to Priya and James.
“Separate for now,” she said. “Not irrelevant.”
At eleven, David joined them to check the commercial model. He had spent the morning reviewing the assumptions behind the renewal price and had marked three lines in red.

“If we hold the fee and keep the existing scope, the contribution stays at eighteen per cent,” he said. “If we absorb the proposed extended weekend cover without changing the fee, it drops below fifteen. That is before any further volume growth.”
“Can we offer a lower fee against a narrower service?” Sophie asked.
“Possibly. But the saving must be real. Removing low-volume activity does not help much if the staffing rota remains unchanged.”
James folded his arms. “Meridian will say the new automation should reduce our cost.”
“It might,” David said. “If it works, if the data is clean, and if the teams stop doing the same checks manually. Until then, it is a forecast, not margin.”

The distinction settled into the room. Meridian’s likely request was for a visible price reduction. Northbridge could not make one safely by relabelling its existing margin, nor could it promise that an untested technical change would pay for itself. But the data showed places where both sides might reduce work: duplicated tickets, repeated checks, and incidents whose ownership was unclear.

Sophie drew three columns on the whiteboard: price, scope, performance. “We’ve been treating them as one argument. We should not. A price reduction needs a reciprocal change—less scope, more predictable volume, or a measurable efficiency. A service improvement needs an agreed baseline. And a concession on one dimension should not quietly become an entitlement on all three.”
“That’s tidy in the room,” James said. “Less tidy at the table.”
“Then we need to be clear before we sit down.”
Priya saved the reconciliation draft. “I’ll mark the records we can verify and the ones we can’t. No blended total.”
Sophie closed her notebook. The evidence had not delivered an easy answer. It had done something more useful: it had made it harder to mistake a position for a fact, or an estimate for a commitment.

Outside, the office was filling with the ordinary sounds of work—calls, footsteps, the lift announcing itself. Sophie looked at Helen’s message once more. Rachel could join the review. That meant Meridian was willing to examine the problem. It did not mean Helen was ready to move on price.

For the next meeting, Sophie would need to understand what the demand for savings was protecting, and what Northbridge could offer in return without giving away the service that made the contract worth renewing.

chapters.title: The Number Behind the Number
pages: Helen accepted Sophie’s invitation for a short call on Thursday, but asked that they keep the discussion “at working level”. Sophie understood the distinction. No formal offer, no recorded commitment—just enough room to say something that might later matter.

They met in a small room at Meridian’s head office. Helen arrived with a folder and her phone face down on the table. She was neatly composed, though a faint crease between her eyebrows suggested the morning had already made demands of her.
“Your note was more careful than most,” she said.
“The data is more complicated than most headlines,” Sophie replied.
“I appreciate that. I still need a commercial outcome I can take to the board.”
“Can you tell me what the board needs to see?”

Helen turned the phone over, then back again. “A reduction in the cost of the service, or a credible route to one. The business has a wider savings programme. Procurement has been asked to show results, not merely avoid increases.”
“Is there a particular figure attached to this contract?”
“There’s a target across the operating portfolio. It’s not a number I can allocate neatly to one supplier.”

Sophie heard the answer as both information and boundary. Helen had not said there was no target. She had said the target was not assigned to Northbridge. That could mean the figure remained under discussion, or that Helen had no authority to disclose it, or that she wanted Northbridge to make the first move.
“If we offered a reduction in annual price,” Sophie said, “what would Meridian be prepared to change in return? For example, a firmer volume forecast, a longer term, or a defined reduction in scope?”
Helen’s expression did not alter. “I can’t promise a longer term in return for a concession you haven’t made.”
“That’s fair. I’m not asking you to promise now. I’m trying to find out which forms of commitment are possible.”
“The business has not agreed to lock its volumes. Store activity changes quickly. A three-year commitment would be difficult.”
“Would a two-year term be possible if the first year had a review point?”
“Possibly. But I don’t want to trade a longer term for a price that remains above the benchmark.”
Sophie let the silence stand. Helen aligned the edge of her folder with the table. It was a small action, but it gave Sophie a moment to resist the temptation to fill the pause with a discount.
“You’re asking for a benchmark,” Sophie said at last. “Can you share what it includes?”

Helen looked directly at her. “The comparison isn’t like for like. One provider has quoted a lower headline fee. Their offer assumes a narrower support window and treats some integration work as chargeable.”
“So the headline is lower, but the total cost may not be.”
“It may be. We haven’t completed the assessment.”
“And switching?”

“There would be a transition cost. It is not impossible, but it is not free.” Helen’s tone remained neutral. “We do have a credible alternative. I don’t want you to assume that the difficulty of changing supplier means Meridian will stay.”
Sophie nodded. “I wouldn’t. Equally, I don’t want us to assume a lower headline fee means a lower cost to Meridian.”
For a moment, Helen’s mouth softened into something close to a smile. “That is why I’m having this conversation with you.”

The admission was modest, but it changed the temperature in the room. Meridian’s alternative was real; so was the cost and risk of using it. Northbridge’s alternative was not an empty threat either. It could decline a renewal that required wider coverage at a price below its delivery cost. Neither side could afford to confuse a viable walk-away option with a costless one.

Sophie opened her notebook. “Would it help if we separated the current fee from optional cover and from the work that might be avoided through better integration? Then we could compare the offers on the same basis.”
“Yes, if you don’t present every potential efficiency as money already saved.”
“Agreed. We would need a baseline and a test period. Any saving would be measured after the change, not promised in advance.”
Helen considered this. “That may help me show a route to savings. But the board still expects a result this year.”
“Would a capped service credit count?”
“A credit is not a saving if the underlying service is poor.”
“No. And we wouldn’t propose one as a substitute for fixing the service. But if the baseline is agreed, a limited credit could give Meridian protection while we test the integration work.”
“That would depend on the threshold, the cap, and what happens if a system outside your control causes the failure.”
“Of course.”
Helen closed the folder. “I’m not agreeing to a credit. I’m saying it could be considered as part of a complete package.”
“Understood.” Sophie wrote that down—not the possibility alone, but its limits. She would not take it back to Northbridge as approval.
When they returned to the savings programme, Helen’s caution became more personal without becoming confessional.

“I have to show that procurement has challenged the cost,” she said. “There are people who think renewal is simply the easiest option. If I recommend Northbridge at the current rate, I need to explain why that is better value than the alternative, and why the risk of transition is being priced sensibly rather than used as an excuse.”
Sophie recognised the pressure. “And if you recommend a change, you have to explain why the apparent saving justifies the transition risk.”
“Yes.” Helen’s answer came quickly. “I don’t want a failed migration on my record because everyone liked a lower first-page number.”

There it was: not a hidden wish for a discount, but a need for an account she could defend. The contract was important to both companies, but their internal audiences were different. Northbridge’s finance team would test margin and delivery exposure. Meridian’s board would ask for savings, accountability and evidence that alternatives had been considered.

“Then perhaps the package needs to give you two things,” Sophie said. “A defined near-term reduction where we can identify work that is genuinely removable, and a measurable route to further savings if the integration review succeeds.”
“That sounds more credible than a broad promise.” Helen stood, then paused. “But don’t send me a proposal built on best-case assumptions.”
“I won’t.”

Outside the room, Sophie called James. She told him that Meridian’s benchmark was lower but incomplete, the transition was feasible but costly, and Helen needed a defensible result this year. She did not say that Helen had accepted a service credit, because she had not. Nor did she say that Meridian would agree to a two-year term. Helen had described it as possible, not promised.
James listened. “What can we offer without moving the floor?”

“A narrow reduction tied to a defined removal of low-value checks, if Meridian provides a stable forecast and lets us validate the workload. Then a joint review of the integration issue, with a credit mechanism only if we agree the baseline and exclusions.”
“That is a lot of conditions.”

“They are reciprocal commitments. If we want the benefit of predictable work, we have to say what Meridian receives for giving it. If we want to promise a credit, we have to know what event triggers it.”
James was quiet. “Oliver thinks we should make the pressure visible. Tell Helen we can’t meet the benchmark and put the choice back on her.”
“Has he spoken to Helen?”
“No. He thinks she’s testing our resolve.”

Sophie looked back through the glass at Helen’s empty meeting room. Perhaps she was testing it. But the information she had shared was not a bluff; it was a map of the decision she had to take inside Meridian.
“I’ll think about the wording,” Sophie said.

As she ended the call, she knew she would have to choose between a posture that looked strong and a question that might reveal more. Oliver’s method had an appeal: it reduced ambiguity by forcing a decision. It also risked turning the first honest conversation into a test of nerve.

chapters.title: The Cost of a Hard Line
pages: Oliver Grant arrived for the Friday negotiation carrying a slim folder and the confidence of a man who believed the other side was always waiting for permission to take more.

“Don’t give them another workshop,” he said as Sophie reviewed the agenda. “They have the data. They have the alternative. They know our position. If you keep asking what they need, they’ll hear that we’re prepared to solve their problem at our expense.”
“We are prepared to solve some of their problems,” Sophie said. “Not all of them, and not without a return.”
“Then make the return explicit. Put down a number and make them react.”

James supported the approach. Meridian’s renewal timetable was tightening, and the board meeting was six weeks away. Northbridge had spent two sessions explaining its costs and another examining tickets. At some point, a negotiation had to reach an offer.

Sophie agreed to give Oliver’s proposal a try. She and David had modelled a reduction of £120,000 per year, but only if Meridian removed the extended manual verification work, accepted a two-year term with a review after twelve months, and provided a monthly volume forecast. The lower fee did not reflect a sudden improvement in Northbridge’s margin; it reflected work that would no longer be done and a more predictable delivery plan.

They put the offer on the table early. Sophie described the current annual fee, the proposed reduction, and the conditions. The figures were set out in a one-page schedule: £4.8 million falling to £4.68 million, before any optional weekend cover. A two-year term would begin on renewal, with a joint review after the first year. The scope change was listed in an annex, not buried in the price.
Helen read the page without comment. Rachel, beside her, marked the annex with a pencil. David watched both of them. Oliver sat back, hands folded.
“If the verification work is removed,” Helen said, “who takes responsibility for an incorrect stock feed that passes through the automated check?”
“The system owner, once the failure point is established,” Sophie replied. “The current manual review is not a contractual guarantee that every feed is correct.”
“But your offer removes a check we rely on.”
“It removes a process that has not been reliably reducing the incidents. The ticket evidence suggests that some of the same checks are being repeated on both sides.”
Rachel looked up. “It suggests that for some stores. It doesn’t show that the checks are redundant for all of them.”
Sophie heard the weakness in her own case before Oliver could speak. Priya’s analysis had identified duplication in some records, not proved that every verification task could be removed safely.
Helen set down the page. “I can take this away. I can’t recommend a two-year term in exchange for a reduction that transfers risk to our operations team.”
“The reduction is conditional on the scope change,” Sophie said. “We can’t reduce the price and keep the same work.”
“I understand the commercial logic,” Helen replied. “I’m not accepting the assumption that the work can be removed yet.”

Oliver leaned forward. “If Meridian wants the current scope at the current price, that remains available. But we cannot reserve capacity while the organisation compares us with a lower service model.”
He had spoken evenly, but the sentence altered the room. Helen’s gaze moved from him to Sophie. “Are you saying Northbridge is withdrawing the renewal offer?”
“No,” Sophie said. “The existing scope and current fee remain available. The reduced price applies only to the reduced scope and the commitments on the page.”
“Then we agree on that much,” Helen said. “But we do not have a basis for agreeing that the work can safely disappear.”
Oliver’s jaw tightened. “This is why suppliers end up giving concessions without receiving anything.”
Sophie wanted to interrupt. Instead she kept her hands still and let Helen answer.

“A lower fee is not a concession if we pay for it in operational exposure,” Helen said. “A two-year term is not free to Meridian. It limits our ability to use the alternative if the service underperforms.”

That was the minor point they won: Helen agreed that any comparison of the offers would list scope, service hours and chargeable integration work alongside headline price. She would not allow the competing quote to be presented internally as equivalent without those qualifications. It was useful. It was not an agreement on value or volume.

The meeting ended with the offer still open and a request for more detail about the removed checks. As they packed their papers, Rachel gathered the marked annex and said, “We should look at the overnight feed before we decide what can be cut.”
Sophie nodded. “That makes sense.”
Helen’s reply was cooler. “It would have been helpful to establish that before a reduction was attached to it.”

The observation stayed with Sophie after the Meridian team had left. Oliver called the exchange a successful test of resolve. They had held their price and secured a more honest comparison with the alternative. But they had also made a modest proposal sound like a verdict on Meridian’s operational judgement.
“She’ll come back,” Oliver said. “They need us.”
“They have an alternative,” Sophie said.
“A costly one.”
“Costly isn’t the same as impossible.”
James intervened before Oliver could reply. “We have the next technical review on Tuesday. Let’s not lose sight of what we got.”

On Monday, Helen sent a short email confirming that Meridian would compare the offers on a like-for-like basis. She also asked Northbridge not to circulate the proposed price reduction as though Meridian had accepted the associated scope change. Sophie replied that it would not be represented as an agreement.

The message was reasonable. Its tone was not warm. In earlier exchanges, Helen had asked questions about process and suggested who should attend. Now she sent precise instructions and copied in a member of Meridian’s legal team. The trust between them had not broken, but it had become narrower.
Sophie took the email to James. “I think we were right to separate the fee from the scope. We were wrong to use the offer as a test of whether she would commit.”
“You didn’t say it was a test,” James said.
“The structure said it for us. The reduction was contingent on a change we hadn’t validated. We made it harder for her to explore the problem without appearing to concede.”
James read Helen’s message. “Oliver will say this is what negotiating feels like.”
“Negotiating can feel uncomfortable without being needlessly defensive.”

Oliver joined them a few minutes later. Sophie did not accuse him of damaging the relationship. She described the sequence: Meridian had agreed to a like-for-like comparison, declined the proposed scope change, and requested that Northbridge keep the unaccepted offer separate from any record of agreed terms.
“We won the comparability point,” Oliver said.
“Yes. And lost room to test the scope.”
“They could have accepted the lower price.”
“They could not responsibly accept the risk attached to it. Rachel identified a genuine gap in our evidence.”
Oliver tapped the folder. “If you keep treating every objection as information, you’ll never get a decision.”
“And if we treat every objection as resistance, we won’t know which problem we’re solving.”

There was no immediate answer. James ended the discussion by asking Sophie to lead Tuesday’s technical review. It was a sensible choice: Martin Lewis, Northbridge’s technical lead, had raised the overnight integration issue before, and Sophie had not yet heard his full explanation.

That afternoon, she reviewed the ticket sample again. The data supported Northbridge’s case that response times had improved. It also exposed gaps in ownership and record-keeping that made a confident claim about removed checks impossible. The commercial point was not that Meridian should trust Northbridge. It was that both sides would need enough evidence to place risk where they could control it.
Sophie added a question to her notes for Martin: What would we have to see to know whether the verification work is actually reducing risk?
It was less forceful than Oliver’s offer. It was also more likely to produce an answer they could put into a contract.

chapters.title: The Quiet Between Questions
pages: Martin Lewis arrived at the technical review with a laptop under one arm and a printed diagram folded into quarters. He had the careful manner of someone who had learned that a confident answer, given too early, could become a contractual promise.
Rachel and Helen joined by video from Meridian. Priya sat beside Sophie, ready to take notes. James attended, but stayed quiet. Sophie began by acknowledging the previous proposal.

“We linked a price reduction to removing manual verification before we had agreed that the work was redundant,” she said. “That was premature. Today I’d like us to understand the process, then identify what could be tested.”
Helen’s face on the screen remained composed. “That would be useful.”
Sophie turned to Martin. “Can you take us through the overnight stock update as it currently works?”

He shared the diagram. “Meridian’s system generates a file at around half past midnight. Northbridge receives it through an integration layer, checks the format, and passes the data to the stock service. If an expected file is missing, our monitoring generates an alert. If a file arrives but contains values the system can’t interpret, it may be accepted as technically complete and still create a business problem.”
“Who owns the first response to that?” Rachel asked.
“It depends on where the error appears.”
“That sounds like no one owns it,” Helen said.

Martin accepted the point with a slight inclination of his head. “In some cases, that is effectively true. Our agreement assigns responsibility to the party responsible for the fault, but the operational process doesn’t name a single coordinator for identifying the fault. Support may wait for Meridian’s data team; Meridian may be waiting for our integration team.”

Sophie saw James make a note. It was a larger problem than the disputed tickets suggested. The contract’s allocation of liability was precise enough to sound settled, while the working arrangement left both teams unsure when responsibility actually began.
“What happens when the value is wrong but the file passes the format check?” she asked.
Martin paused. “The system may process it. A manual reviewer sometimes catches it, but the review is inconsistent. Some Meridian teams run a second check in the morning. Others do not.”
Rachel glanced away from the screen. “That matches what we see. The checks developed locally. They were never designed as one control.”
The room went quiet. Sophie did not rush to explain the commercial consequences. She waited while Martin examined the diagram. He pointed to a box labelled “exception queue”.
“This is outdated,” he said. “The queue moved eighteen months ago, but the diagram did not. Some alerts still go to the old mailbox.”
“How many?” Priya asked.
“I don’t know without checking the log. I can say that when someone notices the old route, they forward the alert manually.”
Helen spoke after a pause. “That could explain some of the cases we’ve called late response.”
“It could,” Martin said. “It wouldn’t explain all of them.”

Sophie wrote down both parts. The discovery supported Northbridge’s argument that the recorded response times did not always reflect the team’s actual work. It also exposed a Northbridge failure: the integration diagram was out of date, and an alert path had not been properly maintained. Neither side could use the finding as a clean victory.
“What would let us distinguish the two?” Sophie asked.

Martin described a joint review of a representative sample of incidents, including the timestamp when Meridian generated the file, when Northbridge received it, when an alert was raised, and when either team acted. Priya suggested adding a code for the confirmed cause, rather than relying on the first label entered by a support agent.

Rachel asked whether the review would include cases where the file was accepted but the stock value was wrong. Martin said it should. Helen wanted the sample to include both high-impact and routine incidents, so neither side could choose only the cases that favoured its position.

Sophie summarised the emerging agreement. “One hundred cases over six weeks. Both teams nominate a technical owner. We record the four timestamps, confirm the cause where we can, and mark unresolved cases as unresolved. At the end, we decide whether the manual checks are reducing risk, duplicating effort, or doing both.”
“And the outcome doesn’t automatically change the contract price,” Helen said.
“Correct. The review informs a proposal. Any change to price or scope would need a separate agreement.”
Helen looked at Rachel, who nodded. “That is acceptable as a process.”

It was not a concession, and Sophie did not call it one. Meridian was committing staff time and access to its records. Northbridge was committing technical support and a transparent review, including cases that might show its own systems at fault. The exchange created evidence; it did not predetermine who would benefit from it.

Martin folded the outdated diagram. “I should also say that we have a constraint on our side. The current connector is built around an older interface. It still works, but a full redesign cannot be delivered before renewal without pulling engineers away from another migration.”
James looked up. “That hasn’t appeared in the proposal.”

“It’s a delivery constraint, not a reason to refuse the work,” Martin said. “We can replace the alert route immediately. A deeper redesign would take about twelve weeks after access and specifications are agreed.”
Helen’s expression sharpened. “Would Meridian be charged for that?”

“Not if the review shows the defect is within our existing obligation,” Sophie said. “If the redesign is additional work or the current interface is being changed by Meridian, we would need to define that separately.”
“We can’t decide that today,” Helen said.
“No. We should not.” Sophie turned to Martin. “Can you separate the immediate correction from the longer-term redesign?”
“Yes. The old mailbox can be retired and the alert route tested within ten working days. That is ours. The redesign depends on the data specification and on whether Meridian changes its feed.”
Rachel leaned towards her camera. “Our data format is due for review, but no change has been approved. If Northbridge redesigns against a specification we later replace, we’ll both waste money.”
“Then the review should include the specification,” Priya said. “Not just the ticket counts.”

Sophie looked around the room. “Let me check I have this right. Northbridge will correct the alert route within ten working days and provide the test results. Meridian will share the current feed specification and nominate someone to confirm whether a change is planned. The joint sample will then tell us which incidents belong to the route, the data, or the hand-off. We are not agreeing now that a redesign is included or chargeable.”
“That’s right,” Helen said. Her tone had lost some of its edge. “I can work with that distinction.”

The phrase mattered. Helen had not suddenly become trusting, but she had stopped preparing for every sentence as though it concealed a price increase. When Sophie asked what evidence Meridian’s board would accept as a credible route to savings, Helen answered more fully than she had before.

“They’ll want an amount they can see, not only an improvement in process. But I can present a verified cost reduction as part of the renewal if we can show how it was calculated and what service was retained.”
“Would a reduction in manual checking count if Meridian keeps the ability to request it for high-risk periods?”
“Potentially. It would have to be a defined option, with notice and a price. We cannot leave it as an informal promise.”

Sophie repeated the point in her own words: “A lower base fee for a narrower, tested service; optional additional cover at an agreed rate; and no claim of savings until the workload has been measured.”
Helen thought for a moment. “Yes. That is closer to something I could take forward.”

It was the first clear description of a commercial structure Meridian might support. Sophie resisted the urge to move immediately to numbers. The six-week review would not fit neatly into the remaining timetable unless it began soon. The technical work could start at once, but the price proposal would need to distinguish interim arrangements from final terms.
“We can send a draft process tomorrow,” Sophie said. “Not a revised offer. Just the review, owners, data fields and timetable.”
“Please do,” Helen replied. “And keep the existing fee and service in place while we review. I don’t want a gap in cover.”
“Agreed, subject to the current contract.” Sophie glanced at David, who gave a small nod.
When the call ended, James remained by the screen. “That was more productive than Friday.”
“Because we stopped trying to price a conclusion before we had one,” Priya said.
Martin picked up his diagram. “I’ll update it. Properly this time.”

Sophie closed her notebook. The silence she had allowed had not produced a dramatic revelation, only an old mailbox, an outdated interface and a workable test. Yet those details changed the negotiation. They gave both sides a way to examine risk without pretending it belonged entirely to the other.

There was still no agreed renewal price, no commitment to a two-year term, and no guarantee that the review would reveal savings. But Helen had described what she needed to recommend a credible outcome. Sophie had learned that the route to a deal might begin not with a stronger position, but with a question precise enough for the other side to answer honestly.

chapters.title: The Terms of Staying
pages: The silence after Helen’s last question lasted long enough for the ventilation to become noticeable. Sophie had learnt that a pause could be a form of pressure, but this one did not feel staged. Across the table, David had stopped turning his pen. Helen’s papers were aligned in a careful stack, though one corner had begun to lift.
“If you cannot provide continuous cover for the price in your proposal,” Helen said, “I need to understand what you can provide. Not what you hope to provide after the first quarter.”

Sophie glanced at James. He had the cost model open on his laptop, its neat columns less reassuring than they had looked the previous evening. “We can offer a stronger service than the current one,” she said, “but I don’t want to describe it as twenty-four-seven support if we can’t staff that promise reliably.”
David leaned back. “That is the first sentence today I believe without qualification.”

Helen’s expression did not change, but the remark landed. Sophie felt the temptation to defend the proposal—to explain the hours already spent modelling, the margin already surrendered in the first round. Instead, she set her pen down.

“The distinction matters,” James said. “A staffed, continuous response service has a different cost base from an on-call arrangement. We priced the latter with a daytime operating team and a defined out-of-hours escalation rota. The document did not make that distinction clear enough.”
Helen looked at the schedule. “The headline says 24/7 service.”
“Then the headline is wrong,” Sophie said. “We should correct it.”
The admission seemed to unsettle Helen more than a defence would have done. She turned to David. “What do you actually need overnight?”

He took a moment. “If the ordering platform is unavailable, our stores need someone to acknowledge the incident and begin diagnosis within thirty minutes. Restoration can take longer, depending on the cause. For routine queries, next-day response is acceptable. We don’t need a senior engineer sitting beside a telephone at three in the morning.”
“But the current contract gives us a two-hour acknowledgement,” Helen said.

“And we miss it whenever the problem arrives on a Sunday.” David’s voice remained level. “That is why I want the improvement. I don’t want a promise that looks better in a tender response and fails in practice.”

Sophie wrote three headings on the whiteboard: urgency, coverage, responsibility. “Then we need to separate the service levels rather than bundle them. Critical incidents: acknowledgement within thirty minutes, round the clock, with an agreed escalation path. High-priority issues: one-hour acknowledgement during extended support hours. Everything else: next business day.”
“Extended support hours meaning?” Helen asked.
“Seven in the morning until ten at night, Monday to Saturday, with the critical rota available at all times.”
“That is not the same as full cover,” Helen said.
“No,” Sophie replied. “It is more honest, and more likely to work.”
James added, “We would also need Meridian to nominate an incident lead at all times. Our team can’t safely act on conflicting instructions from a store manager, a regional director and head office.”
David nodded once. “That is fair. We can establish a single duty contact. But I want the escalation rules tested before the holiday trading period.”
Helen drew a line beneath a note. “And the price?”
James did not answer immediately. “It depends on the term, the scope and the implementation sequence. I won’t pretend it doesn’t.”

The current proposal showed an annual fee of £1.86 million, including implementation and the expanded support commitment. James explained that implementation was a one-off £240,000, while the recurring service charge was £1.62 million a year. Revenue, he stressed, was not contribution: after staffing, hosting and subcontractor costs, the margin on the proposed service was already narrow.
Helen looked at the recurring figure. “It is still above our current spend.”
“Yes,” said Sophie. “And the current spend does not buy the service you have just described.”
“You are asking us to fund a better service when we have been told to reduce supplier costs.”

“I understand.” Sophie kept her voice even. “That makes the shape of the contract important. We may be able to change the timing of the investment, or what sits inside the service. We cannot make the same people deliver more hours for less money without increasing the risk of failure.”
David looked at Helen. “A lower number is useful only if the stores can depend on it.”
Helen’s reply came quickly. “And reliability is not an excuse for an open-ended increase.”
Neither was wrong. Sophie had thought of the meeting as a contest over a number; it was becoming a negotiation among people whose definitions of risk did not match.

On the walk back to Northbridge’s office, James shut his laptop only after they had passed reception. “We need to decide what we can walk away from,” he said. “Not as a threat. As a real alternative.”

Their best alternative was not attractive. Northbridge could retain some smaller accounts, redirect a few specialists and pursue new work, but losing Meridian would leave a gap in utilisation and weaken a reference that mattered in the retail sector. Yet accepting a loss-making contract would consume the very people those other accounts needed.
“We can’t promise full overnight cover at this price,” Sophie said.
“We also can’t treat the headline fee as the whole story,” James said. “Payment timing is part of the cost. If they insist on sixty days, we finance the work before we’re paid.”
Sophie looked at the rain moving across the office windows. “Then we offer a service we can stand behind, and make any price movement conditional on something that changes the economics.”
“Term, scope, payment,” James said. “Not a discount for being asked twice.”
She nodded. Their first useful concession would have to come with a reciprocal commitment. Otherwise it would merely disguise a weaker contract.

chapters.title: The Other Side of the Table
pages: At Meridian’s headquarters, Helen presented the revised service outline to David and Martin, the finance director. Priya, Northbridge’s account director, had sent it that morning with a note correcting the 24/7 wording. That correction was precise and uncomfortable. It made the original proposal look less dependable, but it also made the negotiation more credible.

Martin read the first page twice. “We have a budget ceiling of £1.7 million this year,” he said. “That includes transition. I cannot put another two hundred thousand into the plan because the supplier has discovered its own staffing costs.”
“The transition cost is one-off,” Helen said. “The annual fee is a separate question.”
“Cash is still cash.” Martin tapped the figure. “And this is not the only renewal on my desk.”

David leaned forward. “If we keep the existing service, we keep the existing failure pattern. Stores will continue to call regional managers because the support route is unreliable. That costs us too, although it does not appear on this contract.”
“I know,” Martin said. “I am not disputing the operational problem. I am disputing the assumption that this is the only way to fix it.”

Helen had expected Martin to resist the fee. What she had not expected was his focus on the one-off implementation charge. “Could we phase the change?” she asked. “Keep the essential platform work now and move the reporting enhancements into the second stage?”
David frowned. “The reporting is how we distinguish an isolated store issue from a wider failure. If you defer that, you make incidents harder to diagnose.”
“I said enhancements, not the basic incident dashboard.”
“The distinction has not been clear in the proposal.”
Martin looked from one to the other. “Then clarify it. We have room to move the sequence, not to invent money.”

Helen understood the real boundary. Martin could not easily add to the approved budget, but he could shift expenditure across quarters and consider a longer term if the total commitment was justified. David could accept staged delivery, but not a reduction in the protections that kept stores functioning.
“What if we separate must-have service from optional development?” Helen asked. “A base scope with reliable incident cover, then a priced option for the additional analytics.”
David’s expression remained doubtful. “Only if the base service gives us enough information to act.”

After the meeting, Helen stayed behind to compare the commercial schedule with the notes she had made during the earlier sessions. The quoted implementation figure of £240,000 included migration support, training, data cleansing and a reporting package that had been described as essential in one section and as an enhancement in another.
She circled the reporting package. “How much of this is genuine cost?” she asked Martin when he returned.
“You mean whether Northbridge has padded it?”
“I mean whether the price is attached to work we need now.”
Martin sat beside her. “Their annual number may include a risk allowance. It is common enough. That doesn’t make it dishonest. It does mean we should test which risks we are paying them to absorb.”

Helen remembered Sophie refusing to defend the 24/7 headline. It would have been easier to insist that the wording was a misunderstanding. “If the price was built around a service they cannot deliver, we need a clean reprice, not a token reduction.”
“Agreed,” Martin said. “But don’t confuse a lower proposal with a lower total cost. We still need a viable alternative if this falls apart.”

Meridian had one. A competing supplier had offered a transition plan with a lower first-year fee, but it would require a lengthy migration and would not provide the same familiarity with Meridian’s store systems. Their current team could also be retained temporarily, though at a higher short-term cost and with no guarantee that key staff would stay.

The alternative was credible, but it was not painless. A failure during peak trading would be costly; a transition conducted too quickly could create the same operational weakness Meridian was trying to remove.
“We should not let them use our dependence on their knowledge as a reason to pay anything,” Martin said.
“Nor should we pretend that the knowledge can be replaced overnight,” David replied. “They know which interfaces break when we change a promotional schedule. That is not a line item, but it is real.”
Helen gathered the papers. “Then our position is not ‘cut the fee by ten per cent’. It is: show us a scope that fits the budget and protects the critical service.”
Martin raised an eyebrow. “And if they say the budget cannot buy what David wants?”
“Then we decide whether the alternative is better. But we decide with the actual service and actual cost in front of us.”

As she left, Helen knew she had revised her view of the price. It might be inflated, but not necessarily in the way she had first assumed. The number concealed risk, sequence and work that the two Meridian departments valued differently.

chapters.title: A Price with Conditions
pages: Sophie returned to Meridian with James and Priya. She had asked Helen for a working session rather than another formal negotiation. The distinction was small, but it changed what they placed on the table: not a final offer, but a structure that could be tested.

Priya opened with the scope. “We propose three service layers. First, critical incidents: continuous access to the on-call rota, thirty-minute acknowledgement and a named escalation lead. Second, extended support for high-priority issues, seven in the morning until ten at night, Monday to Saturday. Third, routine requests handled during business hours.”
David studied the wording. “Acknowledgement is not resolution.”

“Correct,” Priya said. “We will measure acknowledgement separately from restoration. Restoration depends on the cause and on access to Meridian systems. We can commit to response actions and reporting; we cannot responsibly guarantee a fixed recovery time for every failure.”
David nodded, not satisfied but listening. “Then the contract needs to say what happens while we wait. Who updates the stores? Who approves a workaround?”

Sophie answered. “For a critical incident, Northbridge leads diagnosis and provides updates every thirty minutes. Meridian appoints one duty contact to approve operational workarounds. If that person is unavailable, the agreed deputy takes over. We will document the escalation path and test it before go-live.”
Helen wrote down the proposed test. “How do we know whether the service is improving?”

“Monthly reporting,” Priya said. “Acknowledgement performance, restoration times by incident category, repeat incidents, and the proportion of cases reopened. We would agree baselines during the first month because the current records classify incidents inconsistently.”
“That sounds like a convenient way to avoid committing to a target,” Helen said.

“It would be convenient,” Sophie replied, “if we left it there. We can commit now to ninety-five per cent of critical incidents acknowledged within thirty minutes. But we should not set a restoration target until we have comparable data. We can agree a target after the first eight weeks, with the evidence available to both sides.”
David considered this. “If the baseline shows the target is impossible?”
“Then we revise the scope or the target together, rather than pretending a number is operationally meaningful.”

James moved to the commercial schedule. The revised base service would cost £1.58 million a year, with a one-off implementation charge of £210,000. The reporting enhancements would be optional, at £60,000, and could be delivered in the second phase. The initial implementation would include migration, training, essential dashboards and a rehearsal of the critical incident process.
Helen checked the arithmetic. “Your original recurring fee was £1.62 million. You have reduced it by forty thousand and moved sixty thousand of work out.”
“Yes,” James said. “The lower recurring figure follows from removing the advanced analytics from the base scope and reducing the fixed support hours. It is not a discount on identical service.”

“That reflects the phased reporting work and a smaller training cohort in the first stage. If Meridian wants the full analytics package at launch, the original implementation cost is closer to the real delivery cost.”
Helen looked at Sophie. “You said you could move on price.”

“We can move further if the economics change,” Sophie said. “A three-year term, a named Meridian duty contact and payment at thirty days would allow us to reduce the annual fee by a further £30,000. That is conditional. We would need those commitments in the contract.”
Martin, attending by video, spoke before Helen could respond. “A three-year commitment limits our flexibility. Why should we give you that in exchange for thirty thousand a year?”

James answered without haste. “It lets us retain and train a stable team rather than staff the account on short-term assumptions. Payment at thirty days reduces the working-capital cost of delivery. The concession is linked to those changes; it is not an arbitrary reduction.”
“And if service falls below target?” David asked.

“Service credits for repeated failure against the acknowledgement measure,” Priya said. “With a corrective-action plan first, and a credit capped at a proportion of the monthly fee. The precise cap is negotiable. We do not propose credits for delays caused by Meridian access or approval, provided those dependencies are recorded.”
Helen turned to David. “The scope is narrower than the original promise, but clearer.”
“The night response is better than we have now,” he said. “I still want the analytics early. We have too many recurring incidents to wait indefinitely for the data.”
Martin said, “I can support a staged option, not an unpriced obligation. The first-year ceiling remains.”

Sophie understood the difficulty. The offer was more coherent, but the additional thirty thousand reduction depended on terms Meridian might not accept. Her concession had a price in return, and the other side had its own constraints. No one at the table could simply authorise the agreement they all preferred.

chapters.title: The Space Between Offers
pages: They spent the next hour testing the proposal against the first year’s budget rather than arguing over a single headline. With the base service and implementation, Meridian’s first-year cost would be £1.79 million. That exceeded Martin’s ceiling by £90,000. Without the analytics option, the second-year recurring cost would be £1.58 million, or £1.55 million if Meridian accepted the three-year term, thirty-day payment and named duty contact.
“I cannot approve £1.79 million this year,” Martin said. “Moving the analytics into a later phase does not solve the implementation figure.”

James opened the cost schedule. “We could split the transition charge across two financial periods, but the work still has to be funded. We would need a signed commitment to the second instalment, not a hope that the budget survives.”
“The second instalment could fall after the new financial year,” Martin said. “That is possible, subject to delivery milestones.”
Helen looked at David. “Would a later analytics phase create an operational gap?”
“If the essential dashboard is ready at launch, no,” he said. “But I want a firm date for the expanded reporting. We cannot leave it as an option we may never exercise.”

Sophie marked a line on the draft. “We can make the second phase a scheduled deliverable, not an optional purchase. The scope would be fixed now, with the work starting after eight weeks of live-service data. The fee would be £60,000, payable on acceptance. We would agree the acceptance criteria today.”
Helen said, “That helps with timing, not total cost.”
“It helps with the decision,” Martin replied. “We can reserve for the second instalment if the first phase is successful.”
David was cautious. “I don’t want the analytics delayed because a dashboard takes longer than expected. Nor do I want Northbridge to claim that poor source data excuses a missed milestone.”

Priya proposed a responsibility schedule. Northbridge would configure the dashboard and define the incident categories. Meridian would provide named data owners, access to the relevant systems and decisions on disputed classifications within five working days. If a dependency was late, the delivery date would move by the length of the delay, but Northbridge would have to notify Meridian promptly and show the impact.
“That is reasonable,” Helen said. “Provided the notification is contemporaneous, not added to a report after the deadline.”

The conversation moved to payment. Meridian’s standard terms were sixty days. James explained that the lower annual price assumed payment within thirty. If Meridian required sixty days, Northbridge could retain the £1.58 million fee but not the additional £30,000 reduction. Helen objected that the supplier was asking Meridian to finance its staffing model.

“Partly,” James said. “And we are asking not to finance the whole service for two months before receiving payment. It affects our cost of delivery. You can choose the longer term and lower rate, or retain the standard payment period and the standard rate.”
Sophie added, “We are not asking for a concession without a return. Likewise, if you ask us to lower the price, we need a change in term, scope, or cash timing.”
Martin’s face on the screen remained unreadable. “Our finance team will resist thirty days.”
“Then the £30,000 reduction is unavailable,” James said. “That is a commercial choice, not a penalty.”
Helen heard no threat in it. The clarity made the trade-off harder to dismiss.
After a short recess, she spoke privately with David in the corridor. “Your position has changed,” she said.
“My position is the same. Reliable service.”
“You were asking for full cover at the beginning.”
“I was asking for confidence that someone would act when a store went dark. I don’t need a fully staffed night shift if the rota works and we can see the evidence.”
“Martin is concerned the price was inflated.”
David gave a small shrug. “Some of it was scope we may not need on day one. That is not the same as padding. But we should not pay for a service description that doesn’t match the staffing.”

Helen understood that she had treated Meridian as one buyer, as if its departments shared a single measure of value. David valued operational resilience; Martin valued budget certainty. Neither was a disguise for the other. “We need an agreement that lets both of you defend it,” she said.
“And lets the stores use it,” David replied.

Back in the room, Helen proposed a three-year term with an annual review of service measures, thirty-day payment subject to finance approval, and the £30,000 reduction only if both conditions were confirmed. The implementation charge would be split: £150,000 at signature and £60,000 after the new financial year, following acceptance of the initial migration and dashboard. The analytics phase would be scheduled for week nine, priced at £60,000, with the data responsibilities and delay rules written into the contract.

Martin objected to tying the second instalment to acceptance without a defined test. David insisted that the essential dashboard be available before go-live. James wanted the payment date for the later instalment guaranteed. Priya began drafting acceptance criteria, while Sophie watched the shape of the possible agreement hold and shift beneath their questions.
“We have a structure,” Helen said at last. “We do not yet have an agreed contract.”
“No,” Sophie replied. “But we now know which decisions are commercial, which are operational and which need evidence.”

Martin requested a revised cash-flow schedule. David asked for the incident rehearsal to be brought forward. James agreed to recalculate the cost of the staged transition, but not to absorb the later analytics work without payment. Helen collected the marked-up pages.

The meeting ended without a handshake. Sophie did not mistake that for failure. Both sides still had alternatives, each imperfect; both had named what they could trade and what they could not. The next draft would show whether those distinctions could survive the language of a contract.

chapters.title: The Small Print of Night
pages: The meeting room at Northbridge Solutions had been booked until six, though nobody had said what they expected to have achieved by then. Sophie arrived with two versions of the renewal schedule: the clean copy, which showed the latest commercial offer, and the marked-up copy, where the wording had begun to resemble a map of disputed territory. She set both beside the water jug.

Across the table, Rachel from Meridian Retail Group was reading the service appendix. Martin, her operations director, had brought no papers at all. He had come straight from a call and still wore his headset around his neck. Helen sat beside Sophie, calm and exact, with Priya opposite her. James had joined by video. Oliver was absent; he was meant to be preparing the revised pricing table.

‘Before we go back to the annual figure,’ Rachel said, ‘I want to settle the incident language. Your draft says that an out-of-hours incident begins when Meridian reports a material failure. Our current agreement says when the service is materially affected. Those are not the same test.’
Sophie glanced at the clause. She had read it twice, but not with that distinction in mind. ‘Can you give me an example?’
