Martin folded his arms. ‘A store cannot complete a stock transfer at ten past ten on a Saturday evening. The system still responds, technically. Your team says that is not an incident until the fault is confirmed. Our people are already calling shops and moving stock by hand. From our side, the service is affected.’

Priya leaned forward. ‘If we treat every degraded response as a major incident, we need to distinguish a genuine platform fault from a local network problem or a third-party device. We cannot promise a twenty-minute restoration when we have not yet identified what is broken.’
‘Nobody is asking you to promise restoration,’ Martin said. ‘We need you to start the clock when the business impact is real.’
The difference sounded small in a sentence and large in the risk schedule. Sophie looked at Helen. ‘What would the support model need to do?’

‘First, define the trigger,’ Helen said. ‘Then separate acknowledgement, triage and restoration. At present those are being bundled together in the draft. If the clock starts on a report, regardless of impact or access to evidence, the exposure is open-ended. If it starts only after our engineer confirms a fault, Meridian carries the waiting time.’
Rachel closed the appendix. ‘And this is why the headline price is not the whole agreement.’

They had spent weeks discussing the renewal as if it were a contest over a single number. The price mattered: Meridian wanted a reduction against the proposed annual fee, while Northbridge had been resisting any cut that would make the service unprofitable. But the clause now on the table could turn a modest fee into a much larger liability, or make the renewal look cheap while leaving Meridian to absorb the very disruption it was buying protection against.
James spoke from the screen. ‘We have priced the existing support hours and the current severity definitions. We have not priced an unlimited out-of-hours commitment.’
‘Nor should you,’ Martin said. ‘We’re not asking for unlimited cover. We’re asking you not to define an incident out of existence.’

Sophie heard the heat in his voice and did not answer it. ‘Let’s separate the interests. Meridian needs a dependable response when stores are affected. Northbridge needs an observable trigger and a commitment it can staff. Is that fair?’
Martin gave a brief nod. Rachel said, ‘Yes, provided the definition can’t be narrowed later by an internal interpretation.’

Priya opened her notebook. She proposed three levels: a confirmed platform outage, a material degradation affecting a defined group of stores, and a single-site issue. Each could trigger a different response target. Meridian would provide a named incident contact and basic diagnostic information; Northbridge would acknowledge within twenty minutes for the first two levels, begin triage immediately, and give a restoration estimate once the fault was understood. A single-site incident would receive a different target, unless the evidence showed a wider pattern.
‘That is closer,’ Martin said. ‘But what does “material degradation” mean?’

‘A sustained inability to complete a listed critical transaction,’ Priya replied. ‘We can define the transactions in an operating schedule. If a stock transfer is on that list, a workaround does not make the service healthy.’
Rachel looked at Sophie. ‘Would you accept that?’

Sophie considered the service data. Northbridge could support the proposed model with a rota and a limited increase in weekend cover, but not at the present renewal price if every degraded transaction carried the same remedy as a total outage. ‘I would accept the operational definition, subject to a joint schedule of critical transactions and a review of the service credits. The schedule must be fixed before signature, not left to a later workshop.’
‘A review can become a way of postponing,’ Rachel said.

‘Then let’s make completion of the schedule a condition of the renewal, with a deadline and named owners.’ Sophie turned to Martin. ‘You know which transactions stop a store functioning. Priya knows which signals we can measure. Neither side can define this alone.’

Martin’s expression shifted, not into agreement but into attention. ‘That would be useful. My team has been calling too many things critical because the current categories are vague. We need the definition to be credible in a store at eleven at night, not only in a contract.’

The meeting moved to a practical test: who could raise the incident, what evidence was required, and how the parties would handle a report made before a Northbridge engineer was available. They agreed that a report from Meridian’s on-call manager would start acknowledgement immediately. Confirmation of a fault would not be a precondition to triage. The precise service-credit formula remained open.

Sophie wrote the distinction in the margin: response clock; diagnosis; restoration. She had spent much of the negotiation hearing positions—lower price, broader cover, fixed credits—and treating them as if each were a complete account of what the other party wanted. Martin did not want a penalty for its own sake. He wanted a response that did not wait for a supplier to agree that the problem existed.

At the end, Rachel asked for the latest pricing table. Sophie glanced at the empty chair where Oliver should have been. ‘He’s preparing it. I’ll send it as soon as it’s checked against the service assumptions.’
‘The assumptions are changing now,’ James said through the speaker. ‘I can’t sign off a revised margin until we know the cost of the rota.’
‘Nor am I asking you to,’ Rachel said. ‘But we need progress we can take to our people.’

Sophie promised a date rather than a number. By the time the Meridian team left, the technical wording was less obscure and the commercial position less comfortable. The out-of-hours definition had not been discussed in any of the earlier rounds because both sides had assumed it was settled. It was not. Sophie understood that the contract’s risk had been hiding inside a phrase small enough to pass unnoticed.
In the corridor, Helen said, ‘We can staff a defined response. We cannot staff a blank cheque.’
‘I know,’ Sophie said. ‘The question is whether we can show them the difference without making it sound like an excuse.’

chapters.title: The Message That Travelled
pages: At eight the next morning, Sophie found an email from Oliver marked URGENT. It had been sent to a distribution list that included Northbridge’s finance team and, through an autofill error, Rachel at Meridian. The subject line read: ‘Concession framework—hold the line on credits’. The first sentence said, ‘We can absorb the support uplift if it buys us a clean price close; Meridian will take the credit cap.’

Sophie read it twice. Then she read Rachel’s reply, sent at 7.42. ‘I am surprised to see our position described as something to be “taken”. We have not agreed to a credit cap. Please clarify whether Northbridge has already decided the service terms are negotiable only in one direction.’
The words were polite. The wound beneath them was not.
Sophie called Oliver. He answered after three rings. ‘I’ve seen it,’ she said.
‘I meant it as an internal working note. I was trying to get James to price a package rather than keep reopening every line.’
‘You sent it to Rachel.’
There was a pause. ‘I know. I’ve apologised.’
‘You also wrote that Meridian would take the cap.’
‘That was shorthand. I meant we should offer the cap in return for the support commitment.’
‘That isn’t what the sentence says.’
Oliver exhaled. ‘I understand. I can explain it at the next meeting.’

Sophie looked at the marked-up appendix. The email had made the negotiation sound like a private exercise in assigning concessions, with Meridian cast as a party to be managed rather than a party whose approval mattered. An explanation might correct the wording. It would not erase the impression that Northbridge had been making decisions about Meridian’s commitments without asking.
‘Don’t send another message yet,’ she said. ‘I’ll speak to Rachel.’

She called Rachel, who answered from a station platform. Behind her voice came the indistinct announcements of a train service. ‘I’m not going to pretend Oliver’s wording was harmless,’ Sophie said. ‘He was preparing an internal package, and he sent it to you by mistake. That explains how it happened, not why it reads as if your agreement is assumed.’

Rachel was quiet for a moment. ‘I appreciate the distinction. But the distinction is also the problem. Your internal note treats the credit cap as something you can give or withhold, and our service risk as a price lever.’
‘You’re right that it reads that way. The intention was to trade a cap for a defined support commitment. We have not agreed either term.’
‘Then why did you not say that?’

Sophie could have said that Oliver had made the mistake, that she had not seen the email, that the distribution list was at fault. Each was true and none was enough. ‘Because I should have set clearer rules for what went into the working drafts and who received them. I’ll own that. I can’t make an offer on the phone, but I can make sure the next one shows what Northbridge is asking for and what Meridian would receive in return.’
Rachel’s voice softened only slightly. ‘I need something I can take to Martin. The service issue is not a bargaining ornament.’
‘I understand. I’ll keep it tied to the operating model, not describe it as a favour.’

They ended without a reconciliation. Sophie sat with the phone in her hand until James’s call arrived. He wanted to know whether the pricing table should assume the credit cap. ‘Not yet,’ she said. ‘We’re going to cost scenarios, not smuggle an assumption into the base case.’
Oliver came into her office ten minutes later. He looked tired and defensive. ‘I didn’t mean to undermine you.’
‘I believe that,’ Sophie said. ‘But intent doesn’t fix the effect. Why did you write “Meridian will take the credit cap”?’
‘I was trying to get us out of the circular debate. Every time we move on price, the support language changes.’
‘Because support changes our cost and their risk. Those aren’t separate.’
‘I know.’ He sat down. ‘I thought a clean number would give them a reason to move.’
Sophie kept her voice level. ‘A clean number that hides a condition is not clean. It is a delayed argument.’
Oliver looked at the table rather than at her. ‘I should have sent it to you first.’

‘Yes. And I should have made it explicit that no one sends a client-facing package until we have checked the reciprocal commitments. I let the drafts travel too freely because we were all trying to move quickly.’

It mattered to say it. Not because his error was hers, but because a negotiation team could not ask the other side to trust its process while pretending that process belonged to no one. Sophie had been tempted, in the first moment, to let Oliver carry the whole blame. It would have been efficient and unfair.

She asked him to prepare three costed scenarios by noon: current support with the proposed price, enhanced out-of-hours response with a credit cap, and enhanced response without a cap but with narrower, measurable remedies. Each had to state its assumptions and the commitment required from Meridian. Oliver agreed without protest.

At eleven, Sophie and Rachel spoke again with Martin present. Sophie began by acknowledging the email, then gave the facts: it was an internal draft sent in error; no credit cap had been agreed; the figures were not approved. She did not ask them to disregard it.
‘What are you changing?’ Rachel asked.

‘The process. You’ll receive a single comparison showing the price, the service obligation, the credit exposure and the evidence required for each option. No option will be described as a concession unless it is matched by a commitment or a value Meridian recognises.’
Martin said, ‘Good. But a comparison won’t solve the incident definition.’
‘No,’ Sophie replied. ‘It will show what each definition costs and what protection it provides. Then we can decide whether the cost is justified.’

After the call, James told her the additional rota could be staffed for an estimated £68,000 a year, subject to recruiting two people and adjusting the on-call arrangement. The enhanced response was feasible; unlimited restoration guarantees were not. The distinction was becoming visible in the numbers, though not yet acceptable to either side.

Sophie opened the renewal schedule and changed the heading from ‘Concessions’ to ‘Options and reciprocal commitments’. It was a small edit. It did not undo the email. It did, however, make the next conversation harder to misrepresent.

chapters.title: A Saturday at Half Past Ten
pages: The incident arrived on Saturday evening, at 10.32, while Sophie was helping her daughter revise for an examination. Her phone rang once, stopped, then rang again. The message from Northbridge’s service desk said that Meridian had reported failures in stock transfers at three stores. The system was responding, but transactions were timing out. The on-call engineer had acknowledged the report at 10.41.
Sophie moved to the kitchen and called Helen. ‘Do we know if it’s our platform?’
‘Not yet. Priya is checking the transaction logs. It may be a regional network issue. The stores can still sell; they can’t move stock between locations.’
‘How many?’
‘Three confirmed, one more being checked.’

Sophie opened the draft clause on her laptop. Under the current agreement, the incident might be classified as a limited service degradation, or as a local connectivity problem. Under the proposed wording, it might qualify as an out-of-hours material incident. The negotiation had become a live test of the words they had not yet settled.

She called Martin. He answered quickly. There was a loud, hollow sound behind him, as if he were in a car park. ‘The stores are using paper records,’ he said. ‘We’ve got a late delivery at one of them and no reliable view of what can be transferred.’
‘We have the report. The engineer has acknowledged it and is working through the logs. I don’t yet know the cause.’
‘I’m not asking you to guess.’ Martin’s voice was clipped. ‘I’m asking what happens next.’

Sophie gave him the service desk’s next update time, not a promise about restoration. ‘Priya is checking whether the failures share a pattern. We’ll call you at eleven, even if the answer is that we’re still diagnosing.’
‘And if it’s not your platform?’
‘We’ll tell you what we can establish, and what we need from your network team.’

They agreed that Martin would provide the store identifiers and local contact details. Sophie did not invoke the draft clause as if it were already binding; nor did she hide behind the fact that it was not. She said Northbridge would handle the report under the existing agreement while using the proposed escalation process as a practical guide.

At 11.06, Priya joined the call. Two stores were using the same third-party network gateway; the third had a separate route but showed a similar delay in the transaction queue. Northbridge had found a backlog in a connector service, but not yet the cause of the backlog. The available evidence did not support a simple claim that Meridian’s network was responsible or that Northbridge’s platform had failed.
‘Can you clear the queue?’ Martin asked.

‘We can restart the connector for the affected stores,’ Priya said. ‘That should restore transaction flow. It will not tell us why the backlog formed, so we’ll keep the logs and investigate overnight.’
‘Do it.’

The restart began at 11.14. Sophie stayed on the call, saying little. She could feel the pressure to turn each update into reassurance. Instead, she asked what the team knew, what remained uncertain, and when the next observation would be available. The questions slowed the conversation in a useful way. No one had to defend a guess as if it were a fact.

By 11.38, the first store had completed a stock transfer. The second followed six minutes later. The third had cleared most of its queue by midnight. Martin confirmed that the stores could return to normal procedures, though he wanted a written incident record the next morning.
‘You’ll have it by ten,’ Sophie said. ‘It will separate the timeline, the confirmed cause, the likely contributing factors and what we don’t yet know.’
‘That’s what I need,’ Martin replied. He sounded less angry, but more tired. ‘The operational damage isn’t only a system being down. It’s the time people spend deciding whether they can trust it.’

At 12.17, Sophie ended the call. James had sent a message asking whether the event should alter the service-credit model. She did not answer immediately. There was not enough evidence yet to classify the event, and the parties had not agreed the proposed definition. To award or deny a credit on instinct would only repeat the same mistake in a more public form.

At home, her daughter had gone to bed. Sophie sat at the kitchen table with the incident timeline and checked each time against the service desk record. The report had been acknowledged nine minutes after the first alert. Triage began four minutes later. The system was operating again within an hour, though full confidence in the cause would take longer.

The facts were not dramatic. Their value lay in what they could prevent: exaggeration by Meridian, minimisation by Northbridge, and the convenient rewriting of events once the commercial consequences were known.

On Sunday morning, Priya’s preliminary report identified a queue-management defect following a routine configuration change. The defect had affected a narrow set of transactions; the network gateway had made the symptoms more visible at two sites but was not the root cause. The configuration had been rolled back, and a code fix was in testing. There was no evidence of data loss.
Sophie read the report with Helen. ‘We should tell Martin before the full root-cause review,’ Helen said. ‘He needs the operational facts, not a polished conclusion.’

They sent the timeline and preliminary finding, clearly marked as subject to further verification. Martin replied that Meridian would preserve its store records and provide the transaction logs from its side. He did not request a credit. He did ask that the event be included in the renewal discussion.

On Monday, the teams met by video. Martin described the effect: four stores had used manual stock controls, and one late delivery had needed a supervisor’s attention. No sales had been lost, but the disruption had consumed staff time and reduced confidence in the inventory view.

James asked, carefully, whether Meridian had calculated a financial loss. Martin said it had not. ‘I’m not going to invent a number because the contract has a credit table. The cost was real, but we haven’t measured it well enough to claim a figure.’

Sophie appreciated the restraint, and said so. ‘We’ll include the incident in the service record. We’ll also distinguish the direct operational effect from any contractual remedy. Those are related, but they aren’t interchangeable.’
Rachel joined the conversation. ‘This is precisely why the definition matters. Your team responded well. The contract should not depend on whether the relationship is friendly on the night.’

‘Agreed,’ Sophie said. ‘The event shows we need a clear start to the response clock, a measurable definition of material impact, and a separate method for assessing remedies. It also shows that a fast response can limit harm without erasing it.’

Nobody turned the incident into a victory. Northbridge had found and addressed a defect; Meridian had supplied information and managed its stores. The service had recovered, but trust would depend on the accuracy of the account and whether the contract made the next response dependable.

After the call, Sophie amended the options paper. She added the Saturday event as a worked example, not as a threat or a precedent. The figures did not decide the negotiation. They made it harder to pretend that the clause was merely legal language.

chapters.title: The Value of the Boundary
pages: By Tuesday morning, Northbridge’s executive team wanted a recommendation. The renewal was now close enough to affect the quarterly forecast, and the existing contract’s notice period was approaching. Sophie’s managing director had not intervened in the negotiation; he had simply asked for a decision he could defend to the board. James wanted the margin floor stated plainly. Helen wanted the support rota funded before any service promise was made. Oliver wanted to know whether the client would move on price.
‘They are not one question,’ Sophie said.

James tapped the scenario sheet. ‘The current fee is £1.24 million a year. Our proposed renewal is £1.31 million, reflecting the additional reporting and the price adjustment in the original term. Meridian’s last position was £1.17 million. At that level, with expanded support, we fall below the margin floor.’
‘Revenue is not margin,’ Sophie said. ‘And their price position is not necessarily their spending limit. What do we know about the cost of each service option?’

James turned the sheet towards her. The existing support model, at the current service scope, produced a contribution margin of 24 per cent at the proposed fee. Adding the weekend rota reduced it to 19 per cent before any service credits. A capped credit model could keep the margin above 17 per cent if the cap and triggers were measurable. An uncapped model with broad incident language could not be responsibly priced.

Helen added that recruitment would take at least six weeks. ‘If we sign the service schedule now and start the rota later, we need a clear transition date. We can’t be contractually in breach on day one because we’ve promised a team we haven’t hired.’
Oliver, sitting at the far end, said, ‘Meridian may prefer the existing hours if we give them a larger price reduction.’
‘Possibly,’ Sophie replied. ‘But we need to find out what they value, not guess from their opening position.’

She looked again at the options. One path protected margin but left Meridian paying for reassurance it might not receive. Another gave broader cover at a fee Northbridge could not sustain. The third—defined response, limited enhancement, agreed incident categories, evidence-based credits—was commercially possible, but only if Meridian accepted the operational boundaries and Northbridge delivered them.
‘I’m recommending the third,’ she said. ‘Not as a halfway point. As a different package. We should show them what it buys and what it excludes.’

That afternoon, Rachel and Martin came to Northbridge’s office. Rachel had brought a revised mandate from Meridian’s finance team. The renewal had to fit within a fixed annual budget unless the additional service could be funded from a separate resilience allocation. Martin’s interest was different: he needed a dependable escalation path for store-critical failures, and he was willing to accept a narrower scope if it was clear at the point of use.

Sophie laid out the three scenarios. She started with the interests rather than the numbers. ‘You have a budget constraint, Rachel, and an operational need that cannot be met by a vague promise. We have a staffing constraint and a margin threshold, but we can support a defined increase in response. I want to test whether the resilience allocation can pay for the part of the service that creates the additional cost.’
Rachel studied the first page. ‘Our budget is not a puzzle for you to solve by moving charges between headings.’

‘No,’ Sophie said. ‘It is a constraint for us to respect. The proposal is transparent: base service at £1.24 million, plus £68,000 for the enhanced out-of-hours rota, if that funding is available. If it is not, we can discuss a narrower support window at a lower price. We won’t label the second option equivalent.’

James explained that the rota cost covered staffing and supervision, not a guaranteed restoration time. The response commitment would be an acknowledgement within twenty minutes for a defined critical incident, immediate triage and updates at agreed intervals. Restoration estimates would follow diagnosis. A service credit would apply if the response target was missed, with a capped annual amount and a separate, joint review for repeated failures.
Martin asked, ‘Would a store unable to complete a listed stock transfer qualify?’

‘Yes, if it is sustained and reported through the agreed channel,’ Priya said. ‘A temporary workaround would not remove the incident. But the schedule must say which transactions are critical, and the evidence must let us distinguish a platform failure from an isolated local device fault.’
‘That is workable,’ Martin said. Rachel did not agree. She was looking at the total fee. ‘The enhanced option is still above the figure we put forward.’
Sophie let the silence remain. She had learnt that filling every pause with explanation could make a position sound less considered, not more. Rachel turned the page herself.
‘What is the lower-service option?’ she asked.

Sophie showed it: £1.17 million for the current hours and existing scope, with a modest improvement to reporting but no dedicated weekend rota. The response rules would still be clarified; the larger credit exposure would not be included. The choice was not between a good service and a bad one. It was between two levels of availability with different costs and risks.
‘If we select the lower option,’ Martin said, ‘we still need the incident definition fixed.’
‘Yes,’ Sophie said. ‘Clarification of what an incident is should not be sold as an enhancement. The additional cost is for staffed coverage, not for being clear about the service we already owe.’
Rachel looked at her. ‘That is a useful distinction. It also means Northbridge cannot claim the rota is a concession.’

‘Agreed. It is a paid service option. The reciprocal commitment from Meridian would be the named on-call contact, access to the relevant logs and a joint schedule of critical transactions by the agreed date. The credit cap is part of the risk allocation, not something you receive in exchange for answering the phone.’
Martin gave a small nod. ‘And if we agree the schedule, you will not later say that the transaction is outside scope because the system technically responded.’

‘Not if the agreed test says the transaction could not be completed. We’ll use the Saturday incident as a test case for the wording, while keeping its actual contractual treatment under the current agreement.’

Rachel asked for the proposed cap. James gave the figure, then explained how it had been calculated against the annual service fee and the maximum likely credit exposure. Rachel did not accept it, but she did not reject it as arbitrary. She asked for a second calculation at a higher cap with a corresponding change to the fee. James agreed to provide one.

The meeting ended without a signed renewal. It did end with three clear tasks: Meridian would confirm whether the resilience allocation could fund the rota; Northbridge would cost the higher-cap scenario; and Martin and Priya would draft the critical-transaction schedule by Friday. Rachel would take both service options to Meridian’s finance committee, rather than a single headline price stripped of its conditions.
As they stood, Martin said to Sophie, ‘You’ve stopped describing our request as more service for less money.’
‘Because that wasn’t the whole request,’ she said.
He gave a brief, tired smile. ‘No. It wasn’t.’

After they had gone, James asked whether Sophie thought the deal was close. She considered the question before answering. ‘Close enough to make a careless promise expensive. Not close enough to call agreed.’
Oliver gathered the papers. ‘The lower option is within their number. We could probably close it if we pushed.’
‘We could offer it clearly,’ Sophie said. ‘We can’t push them into pretending it meets an operational need they have already described.’
Oliver paused. ‘And the enhanced option?’
‘It is viable if they have the budget and if we recruit to the plan. It is not viable if we discount the fee and keep the same exposure. That is the boundary.’
Helen closed the staffing sheet. ‘I can support either scope. I can’t support both promises at once.’

Sophie gathered the two options, no longer embarrassed by their difference. A negotiation did not become fair because both parties moved by the same amount. It became workable when each side knew what it was buying, what it was accepting, and what it would have to do in return.

The next meeting was set for Friday. There would be no grand conclusion, only a revised credit calculation, a completed incident schedule and a decision from Meridian’s finance committee. Sophie knew that a viable agreement might still fail if either side mistook a boundary for a threat, or a movement for an obligation. She also knew they had stopped arguing about one number as if it could carry the entire relationship.

That evening, she sent Rachel a short note confirming the three tasks and the assumptions behind each price. She did not call the proposals concessions. She called them choices. Then she checked the recipients twice before pressing send.

chapters.title: The Trade
pages: On Monday morning, Sophie found the revised proposal waiting in her inbox beside a message from Helen: “Before we reopen the price, be clear what we are buying with any movement.” The sentence was brisk, but not unkind. Helen had spent the weekend answering questions from Northbridge’s board about a renewal whose revenue looked reassuring until somebody asked what it would cost to deliver.

Sophie printed the proposal and carried it to the small meeting room. James was already there, tapping a pen against the margin of a spreadsheet. Priya joined by video from the implementation floor, where two teams were testing a release that had nothing to do with Meridian and nevertheless made every spare engineer feel precious.
“Oliver’s latest position is still two-point-one million a year,” James said. “And he wants the full service from the first day.”
“That is what he is asking for,” Sophie replied. “It is not necessarily what he needs.”
James looked up. “We have been making that distinction for weeks.”

“Then we should finally use it.” She turned the proposal towards him. “His interest is a predictable operating cost and a credible route to national coverage. The position is a lower annual number and immediate delivery. Those are not the same thing.”

Priya’s image shifted as she leaned closer to her camera. “The route matters. If we take the regions in sequence, I can keep the existing teams intact and train Meridian’s people alongside each stage. If they insist on launching everywhere together, we need a temporary second shift and contractors. That is not a saving, whatever the headline fee says.”
James drew a line through a figure. “A phased launch means lower revenue in year one.”
“And lower delivery cost,” Sophie said. “Revenue is not margin. We have been treating every pound we do not invoice as a pound lost, while ignoring the cost of earning it.”
There was a short silence. James capped his pen. “All right. What are you proposing?”

Sophie wrote three headings on the whiteboard: TERM, SEQUENCE, PAYMENT. “A three-year commitment. National coverage delivered in phases, with agreed dates and acceptance criteria. A payment schedule that gives Meridian a lower charge while fewer regions are live, then the full run-rate once the final stage is accepted.”
“Longer term in exchange for a softer first year,” James said. “And earlier cash in exchange for…”
“Not earlier than we can reasonably ask,” Sophie said. “Forty-five days from a valid invoice, rather than another argument about what the invoice means.”
David, who had been listening from the doorway, came in with a cup of tea and an expression that suggested he had heard the word cash. “Forty-five days helps, but it doesn’t fund a careless scope.”
“It isn’t meant to,” Sophie said. “The scope is explicit. The sequence is explicit. The fee changes as the service comes on line.”

Helen arrived a few minutes later, carrying no papers. She listened while Sophie walked through the structure. At the three-year full-service rate, Northbridge would earn less in year one than under the original proposal. But the phased implementation would reduce subcontracting and overtime; the longer commitment would make it reasonable to reserve a dedicated team. On the model David had prepared, the margin was modest, not brilliant, and better than the version in which Northbridge accepted Meridian’s price while retaining all its delivery obligations.
“What do we give up?” Helen asked.
“Immediate national coverage,” Priya said. “And the illusion that everything can be done at once without consequence.”
“What do we get?”

“A committed term, a sequence we can deliver, and a customer team trained before each handover,” Sophie said. “We still carry implementation risk. They carry the risk that a later region does not go live until its agreed readiness conditions are met.”
Helen considered the board for a moment. “Do not describe a longer term as a concession if it gives them a better price.”
“I won’t. It is an exchange.”

That afternoon, Oliver joined by video. Rachel, Meridian’s legal director, sat beside him with a marked-up draft. Martin, the executive sponsor, was absent; he had told Oliver he wanted the commercial team to settle the mechanics before asking him to judge the result. Sophie thought that sensible, though it left nobody in the room with the authority to declare a victory.
Oliver listened to the phased proposal and made notes. “You’re asking us to accept less coverage in the first year and pay more once the service is complete.”
“We’re asking you to pay for what is live,” Sophie said. “And to commit to the route to full coverage rather than hold us to a date that depends on readiness at your end as well as ours.”
“Our stores do not get to phase their customers.”
“No,” Priya said. “But we can phase the work behind them without changing what a store experiences once its region is live.”
Rachel looked up. “What happens if one of your stages is late?”
“We agree a recovery plan, an accountable owner, and a review date,” Sophie said. “Any service credit follows the measured impact, not a general dissatisfaction clause.”
Oliver’s mouth tightened. “That sounds like less protection.”

“It is more precise protection,” Sophie replied. “The current language makes both sides argue about what counts as failure. We can improve the remedy, but it has to attach to something we can measure and control.”

Oliver glanced at Rachel. Neither of them answered at once. Sophie let the silence remain. The first useful movement, she knew, would not sound like agreement. It would sound like a question about how the exchange worked.
“If we take the three-year term,” Oliver said, “how much of the price is fixed?”

“The contracted service fee is fixed for the first twelve months. After that, any annual adjustment is capped at the lower of the agreed index or three per cent. No adjustment applies to a stage before its acceptance date.”
“You have not offered that before.”
“Because we had not yet agreed what you would commit to in return.”
Rachel turned a page in her draft. “And the payment schedule?”
“Forty-five days from receipt of a valid invoice. We will agree the invoice format and the evidence required for each stage. No disputed item holds up an undisputed one.”
Oliver leaned back. “That is a considerable change from the sixty days in our standard terms.”
“It is,” Sophie said. “The three-year commitment and the phased fee make the cash flow workable for us. The schedule gives you an invoice you can verify against delivery.”

James, beside her, kept still. Sophie had expected him to emphasise the value of the commitment. He did not. That restraint mattered: they were offering a trade, not presenting an advantage as though Meridian should thank them for it.

Oliver asked for a break. When he returned, his first question was not about the price. He wanted to know whether Meridian’s regional leads could attend Northbridge’s training sessions before their stages went live. Priya explained that they could, provided Meridian nominated people with authority to confirm local readiness. Oliver wrote that down.

They did not settle the fee that day. They did, however, agree to model a three-year term, a phased roll-out, and a forty-five-day payment cycle together rather than as separate demands. Sophie left the call with a list of figures to test and the distinct impression that the negotiation had finally acquired a shape.
In the lift, James said, “You make it sound as though we have given them something.”
“We have.”
“And we’ve received something.”
“That is why it may hold.”
He looked at her for a second, then nodded. “I’ll redo the margin model.”
“With the actual staffing assumptions,” she said. “Not the version where every person is available twice.”
“I know how to build a model.”
“I know. I’m asking you to build this one.”

His expression softened, though not quite into a smile. The distance between them had been made of small things: late messages, unspoken blame, and the assumption that the other person would understand. It would not disappear because they had had one competent conversation. But Sophie could at least stop adding to it.

That evening, she read Priya’s implementation notes. They set out three regional waves, each dependent on data checks, named Meridian contacts, and a sign-off meeting. The timing was tight but possible. Priya had added a warning in the margin: “A date without a customer owner is a hope, not a plan.”
Sophie copied it into the draft as a principle, not a slogan. The proposed agreement was beginning to contain the work as well as the promise. That made it less elegant and more useful.

She sent the revised commercial structure to Oliver and Rachel with a note: “This is not a discount for a longer term. It is a lower first-year charge for a phased service, in exchange for a defined commitment and a payment schedule both teams can administer. Please challenge the assumptions, not just the total.”
Oliver replied shortly before nine. “We will. I can see the logic. I cannot yet say the number works.”
Sophie read the message twice. It was not approval. It was better than another position.

chapters.title: The Measure of Service
pages: The next meeting took place in Meridian’s offices, in a room with a long window facing a wet terrace. Oliver arrived with Rachel and Martin. The executive sponsor had brought a narrow notebook and no prepared speech. He listened as Sophie opened with the operating model, then asked for the proposed service measures.

Priya had travelled down to present them. She placed a single-page schedule on the table. “We have separated availability, response, resolution, and implementation. At present, the draft treats them as if they were interchangeable. They aren’t.”
Martin examined the page. “Our concern is the time a store has to wait before it can trade normally. The dashboard can look healthy while a store is still making workarounds.”
“That is fair,” Priya said. “A response within an hour is not a resolution. We can report both, and we can define which incidents have a direct operational impact.”
Oliver tapped the schedule. “We need a stronger service promise if we are taking a longer commitment.”
“You should,” Sophie said. “But a stronger promise has to be deliverable and measurable.”

The draft proposed monthly availability of 99.7 per cent for the live service, excluding agreed maintenance windows and failures caused by Meridian’s own systems or third-party connections outside Northbridge’s control. Priority-one incidents would receive an initial response within thirty minutes and a named incident lead within an hour. The teams would agree a recovery objective for each service component during implementation rather than pretend one number fitted every failure.
“Why not promise resolution within four hours?” Martin asked.

“Because we cannot honestly promise that for every cause,” Priya replied. “We can commit to continuous work, updates every thirty minutes, and a recovery plan within two hours for a priority-one incident. For a fault in our platform, we can set a stronger resolution target. For a failure in a store’s network, a four-hour promise from us would be theatre.”
Martin studied her. “You are saying our obligation is to distinguish the cause before asking for a remedy.”

“I’m saying both teams need to cooperate in finding it. If our platform is at fault, we own the fix. If the evidence is unclear, we investigate together. Neither side benefits from arguing about attribution while stores wait.”
Rachel made a note. “We will need a mechanism for disputed attribution.”

“A technical review within five working days,” Sophie said. “Escalation to the service leads, then the commercial sponsors if it remains unresolved. No party loses the right to dispute a credit, but the operational response continues.”
Oliver looked at the figures. “What do we get if availability falls below the target?”

Sophie placed the proposed credit table beside the service schedule. Credits would rise with the severity and duration of a measured failure, calculated against the monthly service fee for the affected service. The total service-credit exposure would be capped at eight per cent of that month’s fee. Repeated failure would trigger a formal review and a right to terminate for material, uncured breach under the contract—not an unlimited credit that could exceed the value of the service.
“Eight per cent is not a strong incentive,” Oliver said.

“It is meaningful without turning the credit into a substitute for performance,” Sophie replied. “You also get transparent reporting, a recovery plan, and a review point. We are not asking you to accept a weak service. We are refusing to pretend money alone repairs it.”
Martin turned to Rachel. “Could we make the cap apply to the affected service rather than the whole monthly fee?”
Rachel checked the draft. “It already does.”
“Then we should make that plain in the schedule.”

The room’s tone changed by a degree. Not agreement, exactly, but attention. Sophie noticed Martin had not asked for a larger number simply to demonstrate authority. He had been looking for a remedy that mattered when stores were affected.

Oliver raised the broader liability clause. Meridian wanted Northbridge to accept exposure up to three times annual fees for any service failure that caused business interruption. Northbridge’s proposed limit was one year of fees in aggregate, with the usual exceptions for fraud, wilful misconduct, and other liabilities that could not lawfully be limited.
“We cannot accept three times the annual fee,” James said. He had joined the meeting to cover the financial and contractual boundary. “It would make the agreement commercially impossible to insure.”
“The operational consequence of a failure could be greater than the contract value,” Oliver said.

“It could,” James replied. “But a cap is not a claim that the loss cannot be larger. It is an allocation of risk that reflects price, control, and insurance. We can’t take an uncapped commercial exposure for an event caused by systems we do not own.”

Sophie saw Oliver prepare to answer and gave him space. He had a legitimate concern. The stores depended on the service; their losses would not be neatly limited to a monthly credit. She also knew that accepting a number Northbridge could not carry would make every other promise less credible.
Martin spoke first. “What can you improve?”

“Accountability,” Sophie said. “A named service director, an incident lead for serious events, a written root-cause report within ten working days, and quarterly reviews with both operational teams. For the liability cap, we can discuss a separate higher sub-cap for defined data-protection and confidentiality claims, subject to insurance and the exclusions in the draft. We cannot accept three times annual fees for every service failure.”
Rachel’s pen paused. “You have authority to offer a higher sub-cap?”
“Subject to Helen and our insurer confirming the limit.”
“That is not a number,” Oliver said.
“No,” Sophie replied. “It is the boundary of my authority. I won’t invent a number that Northbridge cannot honour.”
Martin closed his notebook. “That is preferable to a number you withdraw later.”
Oliver looked at him. “We still need an answer to the risk.”
“We need an answer we can buy,” Martin said. “A three-times cap on everything is not necessarily an answer.”

The discussion turned to responsibility. Meridian would provide clean reference data, name a product owner for each regional wave, and give Northbridge access to the relevant test environments. Northbridge would supply the implementation lead, migration tools, training materials, and a weekly readiness report. Each side would appoint a decision-maker capable of resolving ordinary scope questions without sending them to the executive level.

Priya proposed training two Meridian teams for each wave: the operational leads and a small group of local champions. “If we train everyone at the end, we create a large audience and no one who remembers the decisions. Training before go-live gives the people in each region a chance to test the process.”
“That adds work for our regional managers,” Oliver said.

“It does,” Priya said. “It also gives you a trained team at each acceptance point. If you cannot release those people, we can move the date, but not absorb the delay and still pretend the original timetable stands.”
“You are making our readiness a condition.”
“It is a responsibility,” Sophie said. “Just as our staffing and technical readiness are yours to rely on.”

There was no comfort in saying it. The sentence exposed the reciprocal nature of the deal: Meridian could not transfer its own implementation risk to Northbridge simply by calling it a service expectation. Northbridge could not claim that a reliable launch depended only on customer cooperation.

At the end of the meeting, Rachel agreed to revise the schedules. Oliver did not accept the proposed eight-per-cent cap, but he agreed to test it against the credit model. Martin asked for the named-accountability structure in writing and wanted the quarterly review to include trend data, not merely a report on the previous month.
On the train back, Priya sat opposite Sophie and watched the rain drag the city into grey streaks. “I think Martin understood the problem.”
“He understood the explanation,” Sophie said. “That is not the same as accepting the solution.”
“Do you ever let yourself enjoy progress?”
“After it has survived the redlines.”
Priya laughed once. “You are learning to be pleasant.”
“I’ll try not to overdo it.”

They reviewed the implementation responsibilities on a laptop balanced between them. Priya had marked several points where the commercial draft implied work without assigning an owner. One clause promised that “the parties will ensure readiness” but said nothing about who checked the data, who approved the test result, or what happened if a contact failed to attend.

Sophie replaced the sentence with a short table. Each task had an owner, an evidence requirement, and an escalation route. It made the agreement longer. It also made it harder for either side to hide behind the plural word “parties”.

By the time they reached Northbridge, James had sent a note: the revised model showed a viable, though thinner than target, margin if the three-year term and phased staffing assumptions held. He had added: “No spare capacity for an unpriced expansion.”
Sophie forwarded that line to Priya. “We need a change-control mechanism that works before somebody asks for a favour.”
“And a clear definition of a favour,” Priya replied.

Sophie saved the draft. Service improvement, she thought, did not begin with a dramatic promise. It began with a sentence somebody could act on at half past two in the morning, while a store waited and two teams tried to find the cause.

chapters.title: The Draft Between Them
pages: The first integrated draft arrived on Wednesday with more comments than white space. Rachel had reorganised the schedules, Oliver had challenged the price table, and Northbridge’s solicitor had returned the liability clause with a note in the margin: “Do not trade this without confirming insurance.” Sophie read the document at her desk, then took it to a meeting room before the track changes began to look like a quarrel.
Helen joined her with a folder. “David’s final view is that the deal is viable if the implementation assumptions are protected. He dislikes the payment concession.”
“Forty-five days?”
“He would prefer sixty. He accepts that the phased billing makes forty-five a reciprocal term rather than an unsecured loan.”
“And the margin?”
“Below our preferred threshold in year one. Within range over the term, provided we do not add scope without price or recoverable effort.”
Sophie set down the draft. “So we are accepting a lower first-year margin in exchange for a committed route to a stable account. Not a promise of future growth.”
“Exactly. Helen approved the commercial boundary, not every possible future.”

The clarification steadied Sophie. She had been hearing the phrase “strategic customer” used as if it were a financial instrument. It was not. Meridian could become valuable, but only if the work remained valuable to Northbridge.

James arrived carrying a spreadsheet. He had changed the staffing model to show a named implementation team, a controlled allocation of specialists, and a reserve that could be released only by approval. “I’ve accounted for the training and the review meetings,” he said. “The margin still holds, narrowly. But if Meridian adds a fourth regional wave, that is a change request.”
“Put it in writing,” Sophie said.
He glanced at her. “I have.”
The exchange was almost easy. Then he added, “You could have brought me into the price discussion earlier.”
Sophie set her pen down. “I could have. I was trying to keep the negotiation controlled.”
“It was controlled without me.”
“I thought you wanted the numbers to settle first.”
“I wanted to know when my assumptions were being used to make an offer.”

His voice was calm, which made the point harder to dismiss. Sophie could have explained that the previous weeks had not offered much room for trust. Instead, she recognised that the explanation would not change the effect.
“You’re right,” she said. “I should have brought you in when the structure changed, not after the shape was already decided.”
James waited, perhaps expecting a qualification. When none came, he nodded. “Next time, ask me before the proposal becomes a fact.”
“I will.”
He opened his spreadsheet. “Then let’s make sure this one is a fact we can deliver.”

The call with Meridian began at noon. Rachel had accepted the basic price architecture but wanted the annual fee stated in a way that could not be read as covering work outside the defined scope. Oliver still wanted the first year closer to his original target. Martin had asked both teams to present their remaining issues, not repeat their opening positions.

Sophie shared the fee table. The full annual run-rate would be £2.28 million once all agreed regions were live. During the first year, charges would follow the phased schedule: £2.08 million for the first twelve months, assuming the three waves reached their planned acceptance dates. If a Meridian readiness dependency delayed a stage, its launch date and related fee would move by the same agreed period. If Northbridge caused the delay, the teams would follow the recovery process and the corresponding charge would not begin before acceptance.
Oliver read the table. “The first-year figure is still above our ceiling.”
“It is above the number you asked us to meet,” Sophie said. “It is below the cost of delivering the full service from day one, because we are not delivering the full service from day one.”
“And the three-year total is higher than the annual number we began with.”

“Because it includes the support, training, reporting, and implementation capacity in the agreed scope. We can reduce the total by removing work. We cannot keep the work and pretend it costs nothing.”
Martin intervened before the conversation hardened. “Is there any scope we can defer without creating operational risk?”

Priya explained that the enhanced dashboard could be delivered after the first regional wave, but only if Meridian accepted a more basic monthly report during that period. The dashboard was useful; it was not essential to the initial service. Deferring it would reduce Northbridge’s year-one workload and bring the initial charge down by a modest amount, but the later release would be scheduled and priced within the existing scope.
Oliver asked whether that meant paying twice.
“No,” Priya said. “It means the dashboard is delivered in the second wave rather than the first. The total scope and fee do not change. The timing does.”
“Would that help your margin?” David asked from the Northbridge side.
“It makes the delivery plan less congested. It does not turn a poor deal into a good one.”
Sophie appreciated the honesty. A small operational adjustment could not be sold as a financial miracle. Oliver and Martin conferred quietly. Rachel wrote a note.
“We can accept the dashboard after the first wave,” Oliver said. “Provided the report includes the service measures and the regional exceptions.”
“Agreed,” Sophie said. “That is a specification, not an additional feature.”

They recorded it. The change improved the sequence and reduced a pressure point without changing the headline price. For a moment, Sophie felt the negotiation take on a quieter rhythm. Then Rachel raised the disputed clause on liability.

Helen had authorised a higher sub-cap for specified confidentiality and data-protection breaches, but only after confirming the limit with Northbridge’s insurer. The approved figure was twice the annual fee, subject to a separate aggregate cap and the statutory exclusions. It did not extend to ordinary service interruption. Sophie explained the distinction and sent Rachel the insurer-approved wording.
Oliver did not accept it immediately. “Our concern is still that service failure can cause losses far beyond the credits.”

“We understand,” Sophie said. “The credits are a prompt and a remedy for measured service performance. The liability cap allocates broader exposure. Those are related, but they are not interchangeable.”

Martin asked whether the service schedule could include a repeat-failure trigger, not just a monthly credit. Sophie proposed two consecutive months below target or three in any rolling six-month period would require a formal service recovery plan, executive review, and a cure period. If the failure remained material and uncured, Meridian would retain its contractual termination rights.
“That gives us a path to act before the year is over,” Martin said.
“Yes,” Sophie replied. “And it gives us a chance to fix the cause before the relationship becomes a calculation of credits.”

Rachel asked for the wording to be tied to the same measurement definitions used in the monthly report. Sophie agreed. It was a small point, but one that prevented the remedy from resting on a different definition of failure than the service promise.

By late afternoon, the open items fit on one page. The annual fee and phased schedule were agreed in principle. The three-year term was accepted, with termination rights for material breach and a mutual review before any optional extension. Payment at forty-five days was accepted, provided invoices followed the agreed evidence template and undisputed amounts remained payable while a specific item was investigated.

The eight-per-cent monthly service-credit cap remained under discussion. Meridian wanted credits to roll forward when a serious incident occurred near a month-end. Northbridge did not want one incident to generate an unbounded liability through a calculation repeated over several periods.

Sophie suggested a single credit assessment for the incident, measured by its duration and impact, with the credit applied to the next invoice if the month’s invoice had already been issued. The monthly cap would remain eight per cent of the affected service fee; a separate recovery and termination process would address repeated failures.
Oliver said, “That sounds tidy for you.”

“It is tidy for both sides,” Sophie said. “It means the same incident is not counted twice because it crossed a billing date. It also means a failure that continues into the next month is measured in both months.”
Rachel checked the example. “That is fair, if the end time is recorded consistently.”

Priya offered an incident log visible to both service teams. The log would record detection, acknowledgement, updates, workarounds, restoration, and the best-supported cause. Where the cause remained uncertain, it would say so rather than assign blame by default.
Martin nodded. “Put that in the service schedule.”
At six, they ended the call without signing. Sophie remained at the table while James collected his papers. “It’s nearly there,” he said.
“The important parts are nearly there. The wording still has to survive people who were not on the call.”
“That is what legal review is for.”
“And what commercial review is for.”
He gave her a sideways look. “You don’t have to make every sensible sentence sound like a warning.”
“I am working on it.”

The next morning, Priya sent Sophie a note with a list of unresolved implementation assumptions: Meridian’s test data was not yet clean; one regional lead had not been nominated; the training dates conflicted with a major retail period. The contract could not correct those facts, but it could name them and set a route to resolve them.

Sophie added a readiness gate before each wave. At the gate, both teams would confirm data quality, access, named contacts, training attendance, and a passed end-to-end test. Either side could raise a failed condition with evidence. The launch date would then be revised by agreement, and the impact on fees and staffing would follow the cause of the delay.
James read the change and said, “That clause could make us look as though we expect Meridian to fail.”
“It makes us look as though we expect reality.”
“We need to phrase it better.”
Together they did. The revised language described readiness as a joint control, with separate responsibilities and an escalation meeting within two working days of a failed gate.

Sophie sent the new draft to Oliver with the remaining issues highlighted. She did not write “final offer”. She did not call the document a compromise. She wrote: “This is the structure we can deliver on the assumptions shown. If any assumption is wrong, please identify it. The next discussion should be about the risk each clause leaves with each team.”
His reply arrived later that afternoon: “Agreed. We will review against our operating requirements and come back with the points we cannot accept.”

Sophie closed the email. They had stopped asking who could move furthest. They were beginning to ask who would carry what if the plan went wrong. It was a less triumphant question, and a more serious one.

chapters.title: The Obligations
pages: The review meeting was held in a smaller room at Northbridge, with the revised contract projected on the wall. Helen sat beside Sophie. James and David took the other side, while Priya joined in person, carrying a notebook crowded with implementation dates. Meridian had Oliver, Rachel, and Martin. No one brought a presentation.

Rachel began with the issues Meridian could accept. The three-year term, the staged rollout, the forty-five-day payment schedule, and the readiness gates were all agreed, subject to final wording. Oliver accepted the annual run-rate of £2.28 million at full coverage and the £2.08 million first-year schedule, provided the stage fees followed the acceptance dates rather than a calendar assumption.
“That is fair,” Sophie said. “The calendar is a plan. Acceptance is the event that starts the charge.”
“And a delay caused by our missing data does not create a free extension of Northbridge’s capacity,” Oliver said.
“Correct. The teams will assess the cost and timetable through change control if the delay requires work beyond the agreed plan. A simple rescheduling does not automatically create a new fee.”

David looked at Sophie, then at Oliver. “We should be precise about that. We will not charge for the same work twice. But if the delay requires a second migration exercise or additional deployment support, that is additional work.”
Oliver nodded. “That is defensible.”
For the first time in several weeks, nobody tried to turn “defensible” into “generous”.

They moved to scope. The contract covered the Northbridge platform for the agreed Meridian regions, the defined data feeds, standard support, the implementation work, the training programme, monthly service reporting, and the enhanced dashboard from the second regional wave. It did not cover additional acquisitions, new data sources, bespoke store hardware, or substantial redesign of Meridian’s internal processes.

Sophie explained the change-control process: a written request, an impact assessment covering price, timetable, risk, and capacity, and approval by named commercial owners before work began. For urgent operational changes, the service leads could authorise a limited temporary response, but only within a stated cap of hours and with a written record.
“I want to make sure the process does not become a wall,” Martin said. “If a store issue cannot wait for a committee, the team has to act.”
“They can act to contain an incident,” Priya said. “They cannot build a new permanent feature on the assumption that the contract will catch up later.”
Martin accepted that distinction. The agreement would allow immediate containment and investigation, while permanent scope changes required approval.

The service measures took longer. Meridian wanted availability measured across the whole service, including its own network connections. Priya showed how that would make Northbridge responsible for outages it could neither observe nor repair. Instead, the schedule divided the measure into the Northbridge platform, agreed interfaces, and customer-controlled elements. A shared dashboard would show each separately, with a combined operational view.
“That gives us three places to point fingers,” Oliver said.

“Only if the teams use it that way,” Priya replied. “The incident lead remains responsible for coordinating the response, even when the fault is outside our platform. Ownership of the repair is not the same as ownership of the conversation.”

Sophie added, “A Meridian-controlled fault will not count against Northbridge’s availability target. But we will not leave your team to manage it alone if it disrupts stores. We will support diagnosis and coordinate with the relevant supplier within the contracted scope.”

Rachel accepted the division, subject to clear evidence and a joint technical review where attribution was disputed. The service schedule now had an owner for every response, even where it did not assign blame.

The liability clause remained less comfortable. Meridian accepted the general cap at one year of fees in aggregate and the separate two-times annual-fee sub-cap for specified data-protection and confidentiality claims, subject to the stated exclusions. It would not receive a three-times cap for all service failures. Northbridge would not accept one.
Martin asked, “If the same serious failure happens repeatedly, what protects Meridian beyond the credits?”

“The recovery plan and termination trigger,” Sophie said. “Two consecutive months below target, or three in a rolling six-month period, requires executive review and a documented cure plan. If a material failure remains uncured after the agreed period, your termination rights apply.”
“And if it is fixed, then happens again?”
“The rolling test continues. We cannot make the service-credit cap disappear by calling the same failure a new event, but we can make repeated failure matter contractually.”
Oliver took a moment. “I can live with that if the reports are complete and the review includes the incident history.”
“They will,” Priya said.

The credit table was accepted at eight per cent of the affected monthly service fee, applied once to each measured incident, with continuing failures assessed across the periods in which they occurred. No credit would replace a recovery obligation or remove a right to terminate for material breach. No credit would be paid for an event outside Northbridge’s control, but the incident would remain in the record.

David asked for a break before confirming the final figure. In the corridor, he told Sophie that the margin was still narrow. “If the first wave runs late because our internal team is under-resourced, the model will tighten.”
“We have a named team and a reserve,” Sophie said.
“The reserve is not infinite.”
“Nor is our ability to absorb customer delays. The gates and change control are there for that.”
David’s face softened. “I believe the mechanism. I am less certain both organisations will use it early enough.”

It was a sensible doubt. A clause could tell the teams how to raise a problem; it could not make them feel comfortable doing so. Sophie said, “Then the first quarterly review should be about what is getting hidden, not only what has gone wrong.”
David gave a short nod. “Put that in the agenda, not the contract.”

Back in the room, Helen confirmed that Northbridge could proceed on the agreed figures, provided the scope remained as drafted. She did not call the agreement a win. She said it was investable if the delivery discipline matched the commercial discipline.

Martin confirmed Meridian could recommend the package to its finance committee. The lower opening price they had originally requested was not achieved. In return, they had secured a phased service, defined accountability, measured improvements, capped credits, training, and review points. They would pay more as coverage expanded, and they would accept that their own readiness affected the dates.
“There is one more point,” Oliver said. “Our internal review expects a response commitment beyond the initial incident lead. We need to know when a senior manager becomes involved.”

“For a priority-one incident, the service director joins if there is no viable workaround within two hours,” Sophie said. “For a continuing issue, the executive sponsors are notified at the recovery threshold. We should not escalate every fault to people who cannot fix it.”
“Agreed,” Martin said. “But the notification threshold should be objective.”

Priya proposed a combined trigger: a priority-one incident still without a workaround after two hours, or a confirmed risk to multiple regions. Either would prompt the service director and Meridian’s operational sponsor to join the incident call. A further executive escalation would occur if the issue remained unresolved at the agreed recovery review.
Oliver accepted it.

The contract was now sufficiently complete to pass through legal review without pretending every uncertainty had vanished. Rachel and Northbridge’s solicitor would check definitions, cross-references, and consistency. The commercial teams would confirm the schedules. A final signature date was pencilled in for the following Friday.
When the Meridian group left, Sophie stayed to collect the printouts. James picked up the service schedule. “You held the liability line.”
“We offered accountability instead.”
“Which is easier to measure and harder to deliver.”
“Yes.”
He paused. “I was wrong to think the boundary was the whole negotiation.”
Sophie did not answer at once. “And I was wrong to treat your caution as a refusal to move.”
His expression suggested he had not expected her to say it. “We both make poor use of assumptions.”
“Apparently.”

They worked together on the final internal note. James listed the financial conditions: the agreed term, the scheduled fees, the forty-five-day payment cycle, no unapproved scope, and a review of margin after each implementation wave. Sophie set out the operational commitments. Priya added the capacity plan and the named training leads. David asked them to include the cost of keeping a reserve team available.
“That cost was in the model,” James said.
“Then make it visible,” David replied. “If we hide the work, we will later call it unexpected.”
Sophie watched James add the line. It was a small act of repair, though not an apology. Neither needed to make a scene of it.

That afternoon, she called Oliver to confirm the signature process. He was between meetings and sounded distracted. “Rachel says legal can finish the review by Thursday. Martin has the committee slot Friday morning.”
“If the wording holds,” Sophie said.
“It should. I’m not going to pretend I love the price.”
“You shouldn’t.”
There was a faint laugh at his end. “You may be the first person who hasn’t asked me to say I do.”
“I’d rather you knew what you had agreed to.”
“So would I.”

They discussed the first readiness meeting, the name of Meridian’s regional lead, and the information required before Northbridge could validate the test data. Oliver admitted that one region’s records were likely to arrive late. Sophie did not use the information as leverage. She asked for an estimate and a named owner so Priya could assess the impact.
“I’ll get you an answer tomorrow,” he said.
“Thank you.”

After the call, Sophie opened the project workspace and created a list of obligations by owner. It was not the satisfying final document she had imagined when the negotiation began. It was a work plan, a risk register, and a set of promises that could be tested.
Helen stopped by her desk. “Are you pleased?”
“I’m relieved that the numbers and the operating plan agree.”
“That is not quite the same thing.”
“No. We will find out what we have agreed when the first gate fails.”
Helen considered her. “Then make sure there is a way to say so before it fails.”
Sophie looked at the list of names, dates, and evidence requirements. “I’ll try.”

chapters.title: What We Can Honour
pages: The agreement was signed on Friday afternoon, after one last disagreement about the meaning of “valid invoice”. Rachel wanted a definition that prevented Northbridge from delaying the clock with administrative defects. David wanted enough evidence to verify that each stage had been accepted. They settled on a short list: the relevant stage, the agreed fee, the acceptance record, and the purchase-order reference. A disputed item would be identified within ten working days; undisputed amounts would remain payable on time.
It was not the sort of clause anyone would mention in a speech. It was, Sophie thought, the kind of clause that saved a relationship from becoming a sequence of resentments.

Helen signed for Northbridge. Martin signed for Meridian. The renewal covered three years, the agreed regions, and a phased implementation. It included the £2.08 million first-year schedule and the £2.28 million full-service annual run-rate once all regions were live; payment at forty-five days; the defined service measures; training and reporting; the eight-per-cent monthly credit cap; the liability limits; the responsibilities and readiness gates; the change-control process; and the escalation route for incidents and disputes.
No one applauded. Martin said, “We have a workable plan.” Helen replied, “Now we have to work it.”
Oliver gathered his copy. He looked at Sophie across the table. “I still wanted the lower price.”
“I know.”
“You were right not to sell me a number the service couldn’t support.”
Sophie heard the qualification he did not add. He had not said she was right about everything, and she did not need him to. “And you were right to keep asking what happens when the service fails.”
“I expect we’ll have to find out.”
“I expect we will.”

The first implementation meeting was booked for Monday. Before she left, Sophie watched Priya and Oliver compare calendars. They were already arguing about whether a regional lead could attend training during a stocktaking week. Their voices were practical, mildly impatient, and more familiar than they had been a month earlier.

On Monday morning, Northbridge’s internal launch call began with a spreadsheet rather than a celebration. Priya assigned the implementation lead. James confirmed the dedicated team and the reserve allocation. David reviewed the first-year cash-flow profile and reminded them that the agreed margin depended on controlling unplanned work. Helen asked who would report a scope concern before it became an invoice dispute.
“I will,” Sophie said.
“And if you think the customer will be unhappy?”
“I’ll still raise it.”
“Good.” Helen moved to the next item.

The first readiness meeting with Meridian was less smooth. Their test data had arrived, but a field used to identify store regions was inconsistent. Meridian’s local lead, Martin’s nominee, admitted he had not yet received approval to change the source file. Priya showed the examples and explained why the mismatch would contaminate the migration.
Oliver’s voice was tight. “Can Northbridge clean it?”
“We can map a limited set of known variations,” Priya said. “We cannot safely infer which of these records are wrong. That requires Meridian to confirm the source.”
“How long?”
“If we get the corrected file by Thursday, the test can proceed next week. If not, we move the gate and review the effect on the first wave.”

Nobody liked the answer. Sophie could feel the room preparing to search for a softer one. The old version of herself would have said Northbridge would “see what it could do”, hoping the promise bought time. This time she asked, “Who owns the correction, and when can they confirm?”

Oliver named the data manager and promised an answer by the end of the day. He did not blame Priya for the delay. Priya, in return, offered a short working session with the data team to explain the mapping rules. The work was not free of tension, but it was visible.
When the call ended, Priya looked at Sophie. “You didn’t jump in.”
“You had it.”
“I know. It’s useful to notice.”
“I’m practising.”

The first week produced no dramatic success. Meridian delivered a corrected file late on Thursday. Priya’s team worked through it on Friday, and the test moved by three days. The teams recorded the cause, revised the readiness calendar, and agreed that the first wave’s acceptance date would move accordingly. The fee schedule remained linked to acceptance, so the later start did not create a dispute over a calendar charge. The reserve team was used for two days, a cost James had included in the model but would rather not have spent.

By the next review, the migration test had passed. The service report showed one minor incident and no breach of the agreed availability target. Oliver thanked Priya for the data session. Priya replied that the corrected file had made the difference. Sophie noticed how carefully each of them gave credit: not as politeness, but as a record of what had changed.
The relationship was not repaired by signing. It was repaired in small exchanges where people could admit a dependency without surrendering their position.

Three weeks later, a new issue arrived from Meridian’s side. A regional operations manager wanted an additional field in the dashboard before the second wave. The request was reasonable, and the field would help stores understand an exception. It was also outside the agreed specification.
The message came to Sophie with a note from Oliver: “Can we include this as a small adjustment? It should be straightforward.”
James read it over her shoulder. “That is how unpriced scope starts.”
“It may be straightforward.”
“It may also require a data change, testing, and a new report definition.”

Priya had already assessed it. The field was feasible, but Meridian’s source system did not provide it consistently. Northbridge could add it after the second wave, once the source data was reliable. Doing it now would require manual exceptions and extra testing. The cost was not enormous, but neither was the requested change. The teams had agreed to follow change control for exactly this sort of question.
Sophie called Oliver. “We can do it. We cannot include it in the current release without changing the test plan and taking on a data-quality risk.”
“It’s one field.”
“One field in the display. Several assumptions behind it.”
“What are you proposing?”

“We can assess it as a change request for the second wave, with the cost and timetable set out. Or we can include it in the later dashboard release, once the source is stable, with no change to the fee if it remains within the agreed reporting scope.”
“You are asking us to wait.”
“Yes. And we are offering to validate the requirement now so that waiting does not mean forgetting it.”
Oliver was quiet. “The regional manager will say you are making the contract more important than the customer.”
“Then let’s show him the risk and the choices. If he still wants it earlier, he can approve the change.”

The following day, Sophie joined a call with Oliver and the regional manager. Priya described the inconsistent source values without making Meridian’s team sound careless. She showed how the report could misclassify stores if Northbridge guessed at the missing data. The regional manager listened, then asked whether a temporary manual flag could be used for the first month.
“It could,” Priya said, “if Meridian owns the manual entries and confirms them weekly. We would need to record them separately from the automated report.”
Oliver looked at Sophie. “Would that be within scope?”
“A limited temporary workaround is within the change process we agreed. We can authorise it up to the stated effort cap. If it requires more, we pause and agree the next step.”

The regional manager accepted the condition. Priya documented the work; Oliver nominated the Meridian contact; James approved the hours. The requested field appeared in the report the following month, marked as provisional until the source system was corrected.
It was not a grand demonstration of the contract. It was a demonstration of what the contract was for.

That evening, Sophie found an old note in her notebook, written during the hardest stretch of the negotiation: “Don’t let them move you.” She crossed it out and wrote beneath it: “Know what you can move, and what must move in return.”

The change did not make negotiation gentle. It made movement legible. Price could move when term, scope, timing, or risk moved with it. A service promise could improve when the measure and the remedy were clear. A boundary could remain firm without becoming a threat. And a customer could be heard without being granted every request.

At the end of the quarter, the teams held their first joint review. The dashboard showed steady availability, one missed response target, and a migration delay caused by a late data correction. The service director presented the incident record. Oliver questioned the delay; Priya explained the dependency. The two of them agreed on a revised data hand-off date and an earlier check with Meridian’s source team.

Martin asked what had surprised them. Oliver said he had expected the service schedule to be a list of reasons for refusing responsibility. Priya said she had expected the customer to treat every delay as Northbridge’s fault. Both statements were delivered without accusation, which made them more honest.

Sophie listened. She had no neat conclusion to offer. The agreement had not removed disappointment or risk. It had given the teams a way to meet those things without inventing a new bargain every time they appeared.
After the review, Oliver stopped beside her at the lift. “I still dislike the liability cap.”
“I know.”
“I also know what the service director does when a store has a problem. That matters.”
“Then we should keep doing it.”
He smiled, briefly. “That is a very commercial answer.”
“It is the answer I can honour.”

The lift arrived. They stepped inside with their papers and their separate calendars, neither side having won the argument in the way they had once imagined. The work ahead remained considerable. Sophie knew Northbridge would have to guard its capacity, Meridian would have to meet its own readiness commitments, and both teams would have to speak early when an assumption failed.

But the agreement had been made to bear weight. That, she thought, was the art of the deal: not the triumph of one position over another, but the patient design of terms that people could honour when the room was empty and the work had begun.
